intrinsics.h — Compiler intrinsics

__nes_audio_vblank_tick

NMI hook that advances BGM and SFX delays and updates the APU according to current channel ownership.

Syntax

c
void __nes_audio_vblank_tick(void);

Return value

No return value.

Conditions and limits

Include audio_vblank.h and add audio_vblank.c to the build exactly once. The compiler calls its hook once from either the default or a custom NMI handler. Enable PPU NMI. The foreground loop does not call a music update routine.

This four-channel driver is tuned for NTSC: CH1=pulse 1, CH2=pulse 2, CH3=triangle, CH4=noise, indexed 0..3. It does not play DMC or expansion audio. Do not run it alongside direct APU writers such as the effects in audio.c. There is no PAL pitch table or tempo correction.

Do not call this directly from application code. Linking the music library connects it to NMI through the compiler. The hook saves A/X/Y and does not use shared expression scratch. The hook and pitch tables reside in fixed ROM; it never switches ROM banks in NMI. Its preservation applies to the music hook itself; a custom NMI handler remains responsible for preserving state used by its other work.

A record contains five bytes: delay, CH1, CH2, CH3, CH4. Delay 1..255 is the number of NMI ticks for which the new state lasts. Zero terminates playback and ignores the other four bytes. Tonal notes 0..71 are C2..B7 (24=C4). Noise values 0..15 select a long-mode period, and 16..31 select short mode. For any channel, 255=NES_AUDIO_HOLD leaves it unchanged; 254=NES_AUDIO_STOP silences it.

Usage example

c
// The linked audio_vblank.c supplies __nes_audio_vblank_tick().
    // The compiler calls that hook once per NMI. Do not call it in this loop.
    __nmi_wait();

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

The sample plays an original four-channel phrase once. Music continues while the foreground performs integer arithmetic without refilling for 90 frames. “PHRASE COMPLETE / SILENT” and “UNDERRUNS 0 / MATH OK” mean playback finished, no queue starvation occurred and arithmetic results matched. Listen to the captured audio for the pulse melody and accompaniment, triangle bass and noise. The end is silent. The image reports control results; use the audio to assess sound.

Complete example program

Declaration notes (original source)
NMI hook: invoke exactly once per NMI. With a custom handler or a compiler
without automatic audio-hook linking, call it there. Never call from main
or call it again if the compiler already inserts the hook.
Saves A/X/Y, uses no compiler scratch bytes and reads only RAM/fixed ROM.

kitaqfc/lib/audio_vblank.c:150

c
void __nes_audio_vblank_tick(void){
    __asm {
        PHA
        TXA
        PHA
        TYA
        PHA
        LDA nav_paused
        BEQ nav_tick_begin
        JMP nav_tick_exit
nav_tick_begin:
        LDA #0
        STA nav_dirty
        LDA nav_refresh
        BEQ nav_tick_music
        LDA #0
        STA nav_refresh
        LDA #15
        STA nav_dirty
// Advance BGM even when an effect temporarily owns its output channel.
nav_tick_music:
        LDA nav_active
        BNE nav_tick_active
        JMP nav_tick_sfx
nav_tick_active:
        LDA nav_delay
        BEQ nav_tick_next
        DEC nav_delay
        BEQ nav_tick_next
        JMP nav_tick_sfx
nav_tick_next:
        LDX nav_tail
        CPX nav_head
        BNE nav_tick_record
        LDA nav_starved
        BNE nav_tick_empty_done
        INC nav_starved
        LDA nav_underruns
        CMP #255
        BEQ nav_tick_empty_done
        INC nav_underruns
nav_tick_empty_done:
        JSR nav_silence_music
        JMP nav_tick_sfx
nav_tick_record:
        LDA #0
        STA nav_starved
        LDA nav_queue,X
        BNE nav_tick_timed
        STA nav_active
        JSR nav_silence_music
        JMP nav_tick_release
nav_tick_timed:
        STA nav_delay
        LDY #0
// Remember the new BGM notes but do not retrigger channels owned by SFX.
nav_tick_copy:
        INX
        LDA nav_queue,X
        CMP #255
        BEQ nav_tick_copy_next
        STA nav_notes,Y
        LDA nav_bits,Y
        AND nav_previous_mask
        BNE nav_tick_copy_next
        LDA nav_bits,Y
        ORA nav_dirty
        STA nav_dirty
nav_tick_copy_next:
        INY
        CPY #4
        BNE nav_tick_copy
nav_tick_release:
        LDA nav_tail
        CLC
        ADC #5
        CMP #40
        BNE nav_tick_publish
        LDA #0
nav_tick_publish:
        STA nav_tail
// The SFX has its own delay; completion releases its mask automatically.
nav_tick_sfx:
        LDA nav_sfx_active
        BEQ nav_tick_select
        LDA nav_sfx_delay
        BEQ nav_sfx_next
        DEC nav_sfx_delay
        BNE nav_tick_select
nav_sfx_next:
        LDX nav_sfx_cursor
        CPX nav_sfx_length
        BCC nav_sfx_record
        LDA #0
        STA nav_sfx_active
        JMP nav_tick_select
nav_sfx_record:
        LDA nav_sfx_queue,X
        STA nav_sfx_delay
        LDY #0
nav_sfx_copy:
        INX
        LDA nav_sfx_queue,X
        CMP #255
        BEQ nav_sfx_copy_next
        STA nav_sfx_notes,Y
        LDA nav_bits,Y
        AND nav_sfx_mask
        ORA nav_dirty
        STA nav_dirty
nav_sfx_copy_next:
        INY
        CPY #4
        BNE nav_sfx_copy
        INX
        STX nav_sfx_cursor
nav_tick_select:
        LDA #0
        STA nav_effective_mask
        LDA nav_sfx_active
        BEQ nav_tick_restore
        LDA nav_sfx_mask
        STA nav_effective_mask
// A changed ownership bit forces the newly selected note onto the APU.
nav_tick_restore:
        LDA nav_effective_mask
        EOR nav_previous_mask
        ORA nav_dirty
        STA nav_dirty
        LDA nav_effective_mask
        STA nav_previous_mask
        LDA nav_dirty
        AND #1
        BNE nav_apply_0
        JMP nav_done_0
nav_apply_0:
        LDA nav_effective_mask
        AND #1
        BEQ nav_bg_0
        LDA nav_sfx_notes+0
        JMP nav_value_0
nav_bg_0:
        LDA nav_notes+0
nav_value_0:
        CMP #254
        BNE nav_note_0
        LDA nav_enabled
        AND #254
        STA nav_enabled
        STA $4015
        JMP nav_done_0
nav_note_0:
        TAY
        LDA nav_enabled
        ORA #1
        STA nav_enabled
        STA $4015
        LDA nav_timbre+0
        STA $4000
        LDA nav_pulse_lo,Y
        STA $4002
        LDA nav_pulse_hi,Y
        STA $4003
nav_done_0:
        LDA nav_dirty
        AND #2
        BNE nav_apply_1
        JMP nav_done_1
nav_apply_1:
        LDA nav_effective_mask
        AND #2
        BEQ nav_bg_1
        LDA nav_sfx_notes+1
        JMP nav_value_1
nav_bg_1:
        LDA nav_notes+1
nav_value_1:
        CMP #254
        BNE nav_note_1
        LDA nav_enabled
        AND #253
        STA nav_enabled
        STA $4015
        JMP nav_done_1
nav_note_1:
        TAY
        LDA nav_enabled
        ORA #2
        STA nav_enabled
        STA $4015
        LDA nav_timbre+1
        STA $4004
        LDA nav_pulse_lo,Y
        STA $4006
        LDA nav_pulse_hi,Y
        STA $4007
nav_done_1:
        LDA nav_dirty
        AND #4
        BNE nav_apply_2
        JMP nav_done_2
nav_apply_2:
        LDA nav_effective_mask
        AND #4
        BEQ nav_bg_2
        LDA nav_sfx_notes+2
        JMP nav_value_2
nav_bg_2:
        LDA nav_notes+2
nav_value_2:
        CMP #254
        BNE nav_note_2
        LDA nav_enabled
        AND #251
        STA nav_enabled
        STA $4015
        JMP nav_done_2
nav_note_2:
        TAY
        LDA nav_enabled
        ORA #4
        STA nav_enabled
        STA $4015
        LDA nav_timbre+2
        STA $4008
        LDA nav_triangle_lo,Y
        STA $400A
        LDA nav_triangle_hi,Y
        STA $400B
nav_done_2:
        LDA nav_dirty
        AND #8
        BNE nav_apply_3
        JMP nav_done_3
nav_apply_3:
        LDA nav_effective_mask
        AND #8
        BEQ nav_bg_3
        LDA nav_sfx_notes+3
        JMP nav_value_3
nav_bg_3:
        LDA nav_notes+3
nav_value_3:
        CMP #254
        BNE nav_note_3
        LDA nav_enabled
        AND #247
        STA nav_enabled
        STA $4015
        JMP nav_done_3
nav_note_3:
        TAY
        LDA nav_enabled
        ORA #8
        STA nav_enabled
        STA $4015
        LDA nav_timbre+3
        STA $400C
        TYA
        AND #16
        BEQ nav_noise_long
        TYA
        AND #15
        ORA #128
        JMP nav_noise_period
nav_noise_long:
        TYA
nav_noise_period:
        STA $400E
        // A one-shot envelope must outlive its slowest 16-step decay.
        // Length index 1 gives 254 half-frame ticks; index 0 cuts it at 10.
        LDA nav_timbre+3
        AND #16
        BNE nav_noise_constant_length
        LDA #8
        JMP nav_noise_trigger
nav_noise_constant_length:
        LDA #0
nav_noise_trigger:
        STA $400F
nav_done_3:
nav_tick_exit:
        PLA
        TAY
        PLA
        TAX
        PLA
        RTS
// Internal subroutine: stop BGM channels without disturbing an active effect.
// End/underrun forgets the BGM notes without cutting an independent SFX.
nav_silence_music:
        LDA #254
        STA nav_notes+0
        STA nav_notes+1
        STA nav_notes+2
        STA nav_notes+3
        LDA nav_previous_mask
        EOR #15
        ORA nav_dirty
        STA nav_dirty
        RTS
    }

__ppu_mask_get

Return the software shadow of PPUMASK. Use it to preserve rendering, left-edge visibility, grayscale and color-emphasis settings.

Syntax

c
u8 __ppu_mask_get(void);

Return value

Return the last control value maintained by the library or intrinsic setters as u8. This does not read PPUSTATUS.

Conditions and limits

PPUCTRL and PPUMASK are write-only. This getter does not read hardware. Direct writes to $2000/$2001 or custom assembly bypass the shadows. Use the corresponding __ppu_*_set operations consistently. Reading the shadow does not change the latch or interrupt state.

Usage example

c
__ppu_mask_set(0xE7);
    if(__ppu_mask_get()!=0xE7)failures=1;
    __ppu_mask_set(0);

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

The four library calls turn rendering off, load both palettes, clear a full nametable and turn rendering on. The sample reads the palette and cleared table back before drawing. Expect blue copied squares, bars and triangles at y=16, green filled tiles at y=96, and red square/bar/triangle markers at y=208. Each large block uses 255 tiles, leaving the last cell black. FAILED CHECKS is 0.

__attr_set

Write the entire packed attribute byte at 0x23C0 + (y>>2)*8 + (x>>2) in nametable 0. X/Y are tile coordinates identifying a 4×4-tile attribute area. All four two-bit palette fields are replaced; this does not merge one selected quadrant.

Syntax

c
void __attr_set(u8 x, u8 y, u8 attr);

Parameters

x / y

Tile coordinates, not pixels. Keep x in 0..31 and y in 0..29 for the visible 32×30 tile map. Each tile covers 8×8 pixels. The byte arguments are not clamped; invalid coordinates can write outside the intended tile area.

attr

Packed attribute byte: bits 0–1 select the upper-left 2×2 tiles, 2–3 upper-right, 4–5 lower-left and 6–7 lower-right. Each field selects palette 0–3. Values 0x55, 0xAA and 0xFF select palette 1, 2 or 3 for all four quadrants.

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

Direct PPU access requires rendering to be off or the entire operation to fit a safe VBlank interval. These functions do not wait, queue, mask NMI or restore scroll. Prevent an interrupt from changing the shared latch/address during the call. PPUCTRL bit 2 selects a destination step of 1 or 32 per data byte. The PPU handles mirroring and address wrapping; CHR-ROM cannot be written. Set the intended scroll state after access and before rendering.

NESdev: PPU registers

NESdev: PPU scrolling

Usage example

c
for(i=2;i<12;i=(u8)(i+4)) {
__attr_set(i,6,0xFF);__attr_set(i,10,0xFF); // All quadrants select green.
}

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

This program teaches register setup, direct tile/attribute writes, scrolling and separate background/sprite palette loads. The blue band at (0,16) measures 256×16 pixels: its first row repeats a solid 8×8 tile, a left-half 4×8 bar and an eight-row triangle; its second row contains only left-half bars. A solid green 64×32 rectangle starts at (16,48). A red 64×32 region at (144,48) contains an 8-by-4 grid of triangle tiles.

At y=96, blue markers at x=16, 24 and 32 are respectively a square, left-half bar and triangle; a red left-half bar is at x=80 and a green triangle at x=144. These are background tiles. At y=144, the separately colored sprites are a red 8×8 square at x=16, a blue left-half 4×8 bar at x=80 and a green eight-row triangle at x=144. Final scrolling is (0,0).

The image checks 16,384 pixels for the expected shapes and colors, including sprite colors. Separate state tests cover 31 cases: register replacement, status/latch effects, saved scroll coordinates, zero/255-byte transfers, increments 1/32, map edges, zero rectangle dimensions, table selectors, whole-byte attributes and both palette targets. Values of Y=255 are checked as register writes, not as correct scrolling artwork. Evidence is from KUROSAKI with NROM; real hardware is not tested.

__bankof

Obtain the logical ROM-bank number assigned to a named data object or function. This resolves placement information; it does not inspect the currently mapped bank or dereference a pointer.

Syntax

c
u8 bank = __bankof(symbol);

Parameters

symbol

The name of a ROM data object or function whose placement is known to the compiler or linker. A pointer variable does not mean the object it points to; runtime expressions are not accepted as symbol names.

Return value

A u8 bank number. Zero can identify common ROM; it is not necessarily a valid switch-bank selector on every target.

Usage example

c
bank_expect(__bankof(payload)==3,3);
bank_expect(__bankof(callback)==3,4);

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

The sample checks that both payload and callback are placed in bank 3. This proves placement metadata; separate reads and callback checks prove the runtime bank behavior.

The complete program teaches how a bank number and near address identify data, how callbacks cross banks, and how to distinguish the library's record from the actual mapping. All displayed numbers are hexadecimal. BANK IN and BANK OUT must show 02, BYTE HEX D3, WORD HEX 5C7A, and both FAILED CHECKS and FIRST FAILURE 00. CGB and FC display blue text; DMG displays black text.

CALL COUNT is 02: the far_call macro and __farcall each invoke the callback once.

__bankswitch

Select a logical PRG bank through the compiler's mapper-specific helper and update its internal bank state. This changes the mapping persistently, without updating the bank library's separate record.

Syntax

c
void __bankswitch(u8 bank);

Parameters

bank

An unsigned 8-bit ROM-bank number. For a call, it must agree with the function's placement; for a read, it selects the source mapping. Use the target cartridge's valid range.

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

A permanent bank change must not unmap the executing code or its return address. Put this call, bank_switch itself when used, and the code that continues afterwards in common/fixed bank 0, as the sample does.

The library record starts at zero and does not discover the cartridge's startup mapping. Initialize it with bank_switch. Direct intrinsics and raw mapper writes do not update this separate record; bank_get_current therefore cannot verify the actual hardware mapping.

FC switch-bank numbers are logical compiler numbers. Zero denotes common ROM, not a switch target. The helper normalizes zero to bank 1. On SUROM512, only 1–30 are valid: an out-of-range constant passed directly to the switching intrinsic is a build error; an invalid runtime value falls back to 1 and sets the mapper-fault state. Read common ROM directly instead of requesting a bank-zero switch.

Usage example

c
__bankswitch(1);
bank_expect(home1[0]==0xA1,19);
bank_expect(bank_get_current()==2,20); // Intrinsics bypass the library record.
__bankswitch(2);

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

The initial bank_switch(2) records and selects bank 2. Later, direct switching selects bank 1 and reads A1 from home1 while bank_get_current still reports 2; switching back makes home2 read B2 again.

The complete program teaches how a bank number and near address identify data, how callbacks cross banks, and how to distinguish the library's record from the actual mapping. All displayed numbers are hexadecimal. BANK IN and BANK OUT must show 02, BYTE HEX D3, WORD HEX 5C7A, and both FAILED CHECKS and FIRST FAILURE 00. CGB and FC display blue text; DMG displays black text.

CALL COUNT is 02: the far_call macro and __farcall each invoke the callback once.

__bit_clear

Clear the selected flag to 0 without clearing the rest of its byte. Use this to remove one stored condition, such as a temporary status flag. Clearing the same bit again still leaves it at 0.

Syntax

c
void __bit_clear(u8* base, u16 bit);

Parameters

base

Pointer to the first byte of the flag array in CPU-accessible memory. The array is not allocated or initialized by this call. Use writable RAM for set, clear and toggle operations; the test operation only reads it.

bit

Zero-based bit index as u16 (0–65535), not a byte offset or a bit mask. Index 0 selects mask 0x01 in byte 0; index 7 selects 0x80 in byte 0; index 8 selects 0x01 in byte 1. In general, the byte offset is index / 8 and the mask is 1 << (index % 8). For an N-byte array, require index < 8*N and a valid CPU address range.

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

The caller must provide enough storage. There is no array-length argument, bounds clipping, bank switching or automatic graphics upload. A large bit number can select a byte well beyond the allocated array. Keep the memory mapping stable; do not use these RAM-flag helpers as a shortcut for hardware registers whose reads or writes have side effects.

Set, clear and toggle read a byte, modify the selected bit, then write the byte back. This sequence is not an atomic update. Coordinate writers in the main loop and interrupt handlers so that an intervening update to another bit in the same byte is not lost.

FC code may inline a constant index or call a generated helper. Both forms use the same bit numbering and test-result mask. The generated helpers share argument and scratch storage, so do not re-enter them from NMI/IRQ during another helper call.

Usage example

c
__bit_clear(bit_flags,2);
bit_clear_value=bit_flags[0]; // A6 & FB = A2, decimal 162.
__bit_clear(bit_flags,2);     // Clearing it twice leaves it clear.

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

The complete program reaches this step with byte 0 equal to 0xA6. Clearing bit 2 changes it to 0xA2 (binary 10100010, decimal 162); the CLEAR BIT2 row must show 162. Clearing bit 2 again leaves the result unchanged. The other stored flags survive both calls.

Expected FC rows, in decimal: TEST OFF 000, TEST ON 128, SET BIT1 166, CLEAR BIT2 162, TOGGLE BIT7 034, RESTORE 162, NEXT BYTE 130, FAILED 000. NEXT BYTE comes from setting index 9 in the second byte, changing 0x80 to 0x82 without modifying byte 0. The captured FC screen uses blue text on black.

The program checks every displayed transition and shows the number of failures. Set, clear and toggle themselves return no value; their rows display the resulting RAM byte. Separate emulator checks compare all 520 bytes of guarded buffers in 136 cases per platform, including constant and runtime indices across byte and 256-byte boundaries and all eight possible nonzero bit-test masks. These are RAM-state checks, not a drawing demonstration. Physical hardware and concurrent interrupt writers have not been tested.

                    if (TryEmitBitIntrinsicInline(funcName, args, ctx)) return true;
                    return EmitKitaqfcHelperCall(funcName, args, ctx, new[] {2,2}, "__bit_clear");

bool TryEmitBitIntrinsicInline(string funcName, Expr[] args, FunctionContext ctx)
        {
            args = args ?? Array.Empty<Expr>();
            if (args.Length != 2) return false;
            if (!TryEvaluateConstant(args[1], out int bit) || bit < 0) return false;
            // Split the bit number into a byte displacement and an in-byte mask.
            int byteOffset = bit >> 3;
            if (byteOffset > 255) return false;
            int mask = 1 << (bit & 7);
            int[] ptr = AcquireTemps(2);
            try
            {
                EmitLoadValue(args[0], ctx, 2);
                EmitAsm("STA", Mem(ptr[0]));
                EmitAsm("STX", Mem(ptr[1]));
                EmitAsm("LDY", Imm(byteOffset));
                EmitAsm("LDA", IndY(ptr[0]));
                switch (funcName)
                {
                    case "__bit_test":
                        EmitAsm("AND", Imm(mask));
                        break;
                    case "__bit_set":
                        EmitAsm("ORA", Imm(mask));
                        EmitAsm("STA", IndY(ptr[0]));
                        break;
                    case "__bit_clear":
                        EmitAsm("AND", Imm((~mask) & 0xFF));
                        EmitAsm("STA", IndY(ptr[0]));
                        break;
                    case "__bit_toggle":
                        EmitAsm("EOR", Imm(mask));
                        EmitAsm("STA", IndY(ptr[0]));
                        break;
                    default:
                        return false;
                }
            }
            finally { ReleaseTemps(ptr); }
            return true;
        }

void EmitBitHelper(string name, string op)
        {
            EmitHelperStart(name);
            EmitAsm("LDA", Imm(1));
            EmitAsm("STA", Mem(_runtimeIntrinsicTmp0Address));
            EmitAsm("LDA", Mem(CallArgBase + 2));
            EmitAsm("AND", Imm(7));
            EmitAsm("TAX");
            string maskDone = NewGeneratedLabel("bit_mask_done");
            string maskLoop = NewGeneratedLabel("bit_mask_loop");
            EmitAsm("BEQ", Rel(maskDone));
            _assembly.Add(Expr.Make(Tag.Label, maskLoop));
            EmitAsm("ASL", Mem(_runtimeIntrinsicTmp0Address));
            EmitAsm("DEX");
            EmitAsm("BNE", Rel(maskLoop));
            _assembly.Add(Expr.Make(Tag.Label, maskDone));
            EmitAsm("LDA", Mem(CallArgBase + 2));
            EmitAsm("STA", Mem(_runtimeIntrinsicTmp1Address));
            EmitAsm("LDA", Mem(CallArgBase + 3));
            EmitAsm("STA", Mem(_runtimeIntrinsicTmp2Address));
            for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { EmitAsm("LSR", Mem(_runtimeIntrinsicTmp2Address)); EmitAsm("ROR", Mem(_runtimeIntrinsicTmp1Address)); }
            // Fold the high displacement into the pointer; indirect-Y adds the low byte and its carry.
            EmitAsm("LDA", Mem(CallArgBase + 1));
            EmitAsm("CLC");
            EmitAsm("ADC", Mem(_runtimeIntrinsicTmp2Address));
            EmitAsm("STA", Mem(CallArgBase + 1));
            EmitAsm("LDY", Mem(_runtimeIntrinsicTmp1Address));
            EmitAsm("LDA", IndY(CallArgBase));
            switch (op)
            {
                case "test":
                    EmitAsm("AND", Mem(_runtimeIntrinsicTmp0Address));
                    EmitAsm("RTS");
                    break;
                case "set":
                    EmitAsm("ORA", Mem(_runtimeIntrinsicTmp0Address));
                    EmitAsm("STA", IndY(CallArgBase));
                    EmitAsm("RTS");
                    break;
                case "clear":

__bit_set

Set the selected flag to 1 while preserving the other seven bits in the same byte. For example, mark a quest as completed or an item as collected. Setting a bit that is already 1 leaves it unchanged; this is not a toggle.

Syntax

c
void __bit_set(u8* base, u16 bit);

Parameters

base

Pointer to the first byte of the flag array in CPU-accessible memory. The array is not allocated or initialized by this call. Use writable RAM for set, clear and toggle operations; the test operation only reads it.

bit

Zero-based bit index as u16 (0–65535), not a byte offset or a bit mask. Index 0 selects mask 0x01 in byte 0; index 7 selects 0x80 in byte 0; index 8 selects 0x01 in byte 1. In general, the byte offset is index / 8 and the mask is 1 << (index % 8). For an N-byte array, require index < 8*N and a valid CPU address range.

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

The caller must provide enough storage. There is no array-length argument, bounds clipping, bank switching or automatic graphics upload. A large bit number can select a byte well beyond the allocated array. Keep the memory mapping stable; do not use these RAM-flag helpers as a shortcut for hardware registers whose reads or writes have side effects.

Set, clear and toggle read a byte, modify the selected bit, then write the byte back. This sequence is not an atomic update. Coordinate writers in the main loop and interrupt handlers so that an intervening update to another bit in the same byte is not lost.

FC code may inline a constant index or call a generated helper. Both forms use the same bit numbering and test-result mask. The generated helpers share argument and scratch storage, so do not re-enter them from NMI/IRQ during another helper call.

Usage example

c
__bit_set(bit_flags,1);
bit_set_value=bit_flags[0]; // A4 | 02 = A6, decimal 166.
__bit_set(bit_flags,1);     // Setting it twice leaves it set.

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

Set bit 1 of 0xA4: 10100100 | 00000010 becomes 10100110, or 0xA6 (decimal 166). The SET BIT1 row must show 166. The sample sets the bit a second time and verifies that the byte remains 0xA6, demonstrating that repeated setting does not invert a flag.

Expected FC rows, in decimal: TEST OFF 000, TEST ON 128, SET BIT1 166, CLEAR BIT2 162, TOGGLE BIT7 034, RESTORE 162, NEXT BYTE 130, FAILED 000. NEXT BYTE comes from setting index 9 in the second byte, changing 0x80 to 0x82 without modifying byte 0. The captured FC screen uses blue text on black.

The program checks every displayed transition and shows the number of failures. Set, clear and toggle themselves return no value; their rows display the resulting RAM byte. Separate emulator checks compare all 520 bytes of guarded buffers in 136 cases per platform, including constant and runtime indices across byte and 256-byte boundaries and all eight possible nonzero bit-test masks. These are RAM-state checks, not a drawing demonstration. Physical hardware and concurrent interrupt writers have not been tested.

bool TryEmitBitIntrinsicInline(string funcName, Expr[] args, FunctionContext ctx)
        {
            args = args ?? Array.Empty<Expr>();
            if (args.Length != 2) return false;
            if (!TryEvaluateConstant(args[1], out int bit) || bit < 0) return false;
            // Split the bit number into a byte displacement and an in-byte mask.
            int byteOffset = bit >> 3;
            if (byteOffset > 255) return false;
            int mask = 1 << (bit & 7);
            int[] ptr = AcquireTemps(2);
            try
            {
                EmitLoadValue(args[0], ctx, 2);
                EmitAsm("STA", Mem(ptr[0]));
                EmitAsm("STX", Mem(ptr[1]));
                EmitAsm("LDY", Imm(byteOffset));
                EmitAsm("LDA", IndY(ptr[0]));
                switch (funcName)
                {
                    case "__bit_test":
                        EmitAsm("AND", Imm(mask));
                        break;
                    case "__bit_set":
                        EmitAsm("ORA", Imm(mask));
                        EmitAsm("STA", IndY(ptr[0]));
                        break;
                    case "__bit_clear":
                        EmitAsm("AND", Imm((~mask) & 0xFF));
                        EmitAsm("STA", IndY(ptr[0]));
                        break;
                    case "__bit_toggle":
                        EmitAsm("EOR", Imm(mask));
                        EmitAsm("STA", IndY(ptr[0]));
                        break;
                    default:
                        return false;
                }
            }
            finally { ReleaseTemps(ptr); }
            return true;
        }

__bit_test

Read one flag from a packed array of bits without modifying the array. This lets eight independent on/off flags share each byte of RAM. The result tells you whether the selected bit is clear or set; its numeric representation depends on the target.

Syntax

c
u8 __bit_test(u8* base, u16 bit);

Parameters

base

Pointer to the first byte of the flag array in CPU-accessible memory. The array is not allocated or initialized by this call. Use writable RAM for set, clear and toggle operations; the test operation only reads it.

bit

Zero-based bit index as u16 (0–65535), not a byte offset or a bit mask. Index 0 selects mask 0x01 in byte 0; index 7 selects 0x80 in byte 0; index 8 selects 0x01 in byte 1. In general, the byte offset is index / 8 and the mask is 1 << (index % 8). For an N-byte array, require index < 8*N and a valid CPU address range.

Return value

u8: 0 when the bit is clear, otherwise its mask: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 or 128. The result is base[bit >> 3] & (1 << (bit & 7)). For example, testing a set bit 7 returns 128. Use result != 0 to test whether the flag is set; comparing only with 1 would miss flags in other bit positions.

Conditions and limits

The caller must provide enough storage. There is no array-length argument, bounds clipping, bank switching or automatic graphics upload. A large bit number can select a byte well beyond the allocated array. Keep the memory mapping stable; do not use these RAM-flag helpers as a shortcut for hardware registers whose reads or writes have side effects.

FC code may inline a constant index or call a generated helper. Both forms use the same bit numbering and test-result mask. The generated helpers share argument and scratch storage, so do not re-enter them from NMI/IRQ during another helper call.

Usage example

c
bit_off=__bit_test(bit_flags,1); // Bit 1 of A4 is clear: zero.
bit_on=__bit_test(bit_flags,7);  // Bit 7 is set: GB returns 1; FC returns 128.
bit_is_on=0;
if(bit_on!=0)bit_is_on=1; // The same nonzero test works on both targets.

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

Start with byte 0 equal to 0xA4 (binary 10100100). Testing bit 1 returns 0. Testing bit 7 returns 1 on GB or 128 on FC; the sample also converts that nonzero result to a shared on/off flag and checks that the original byte is unchanged. Look at TEST OFF and TEST ON in the screen below.

Expected FC rows, in decimal: TEST OFF 000, TEST ON 128, SET BIT1 166, CLEAR BIT2 162, TOGGLE BIT7 034, RESTORE 162, NEXT BYTE 130, FAILED 000. NEXT BYTE comes from setting index 9 in the second byte, changing 0x80 to 0x82 without modifying byte 0. The captured FC screen uses blue text on black.

The program checks every displayed transition and shows the number of failures. Set, clear and toggle themselves return no value; their rows display the resulting RAM byte. Separate emulator checks compare all 520 bytes of guarded buffers in 136 cases per platform, including constant and runtime indices across byte and 256-byte boundaries and all eight possible nonzero bit-test masks. These are RAM-state checks, not a drawing demonstration. Physical hardware and concurrent interrupt writers have not been tested.

__bit_toggle

Invert the selected flag: 0 becomes 1 and 1 becomes 0. The remaining bits are preserved. Two calls on the same bit restore its original state, provided nothing else writes that bit between the calls.

Syntax

c
void __bit_toggle(u8* base, u16 bit);

Parameters

base

Pointer to the first byte of the flag array in CPU-accessible memory. The array is not allocated or initialized by this call. Use writable RAM for set, clear and toggle operations; the test operation only reads it.

bit

Zero-based bit index as u16 (0–65535), not a byte offset or a bit mask. Index 0 selects mask 0x01 in byte 0; index 7 selects 0x80 in byte 0; index 8 selects 0x01 in byte 1. In general, the byte offset is index / 8 and the mask is 1 << (index % 8). For an N-byte array, require index < 8*N and a valid CPU address range.

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

The caller must provide enough storage. There is no array-length argument, bounds clipping, bank switching or automatic graphics upload. A large bit number can select a byte well beyond the allocated array. Keep the memory mapping stable; do not use these RAM-flag helpers as a shortcut for hardware registers whose reads or writes have side effects.

Set, clear and toggle read a byte, modify the selected bit, then write the byte back. This sequence is not an atomic update. Coordinate writers in the main loop and interrupt handlers so that an intervening update to another bit in the same byte is not lost.

FC code may inline a constant index or call a generated helper. Both forms use the same bit numbering and test-result mask. The generated helpers share argument and scratch storage, so do not re-enter them from NMI/IRQ during another helper call.

Usage example

c
__bit_toggle(bit_flags,7);
bit_toggle_value=bit_flags[0]; // A2 ^ 80 = 22, decimal 34.
__bit_toggle(bit_flags,7);
bit_restore_value=bit_flags[0]; // Two toggles restore A2.

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

The complete program enters this step with 0xA2. Toggling bit 7 produces 0x22 (decimal 34), so TOGGLE BIT7 shows 034. Toggling it again restores 0xA2, and RESTORE shows 162. These two observations demonstrate both directions of the inversion while preserving the other bits.

The program checks every displayed transition and shows the number of failures. Set, clear and toggle themselves return no value; their rows display the resulting RAM byte. Separate emulator checks compare all 520 bytes of guarded buffers in 136 cases per platform, including constant and runtime indices across byte and 256-byte boundaries and all eight possible nonzero bit-test masks. __chr_bank_set

Select a CHR bank. On MMC3 this selects R0, changing the 2 KiB window at PPU $0000–$07FF. On CNROM it changes the full 8 KiB region at $0000–$1FFF.

Syntax

c
void __chr_bank_set(u8 bank);

Parameters

bank

On CNROM this is an 8 KiB CHR bank number. On MMC3 it is a 1 KiB bank number selecting a 2 KiB window: the low bit is ignored, so 2 and 3 both select the pair of 1 KiB banks 2 and 3. Available banks depend on CHR ROM capacity; the API performs no range check.

Return value

No return value.

Conditions and limits

Intrinsic declarations are in intrinsics.h. Include nes_game.h for the nes_mapper_irq_* macros. Select the board at build time with --mapper.

Writing 0 or 1 to the MMC3 bank-select register also clears PRG mode bit 6 and CHR inversion bit 7. Do not combine this with a PRG/CHR layout that requires those bits to remain set. Switching during rendering changes subsequent pattern fetches. The sample checks with rendering off and restores the font banks before displaying results.

These three intrinsics support CNROM and MMC3. Other boards are rejected at compilation. SUROM also uses CHR control for outer PRG selection and does not allow these CHR operations.

Usage example

c
__chr_bank_set(2);
    mapper_result[1] = mapper_read(0x03FF);
    mapper_result[2] = mapper_read(0x07FF);

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

The MMC3 sample displays CHR markers 19/20, 21/22 and 23/24. CIRAM reads show A B A B for vertical mirroring and A A B B for horizontal mirroring. IRQ counts are 01→02→03→03: each of the first three explicit enables permits one interrupt; the count stays unchanged after disable. Each stage waits six frames.

Usage example

c
__chr_bank_set(2); chr_result[0]=chr_marker();
    __chr_bank_set0(1); chr_result[1]=chr_marker();
    __chr_bank_set1(3); chr_result[2]=chr_marker();

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

The CNROM lesson shows markers 33, 25 and 41 after SET 2, SET0 1 and SET1 3. It reads original marker bytes through the PPU to demonstrate that all three names switch the entire 8 KiB pattern region.

__chr_bank_set0

Select MMC3 R0 and change the 2 KiB window at PPU $0000–$07FF. This is equivalent to __chr_bank_set. On CNROM it changes the full 8 KiB region.

Syntax

c
void __chr_bank_set0(u8 bank);

Parameters

bank

On CNROM this is an 8 KiB CHR bank number. On MMC3 it is a 1 KiB bank number selecting a 2 KiB window: the low bit is ignored, so 2 and 3 both select the pair of 1 KiB banks 2 and 3. Available banks depend on CHR ROM capacity; the API performs no range check.

Return value

No return value.

Conditions and limits

Intrinsic declarations are in intrinsics.h. Include nes_game.h for the nes_mapper_irq_* macros. Select the board at build time with --mapper.

Writing 0 or 1 to the MMC3 bank-select register also clears PRG mode bit 6 and CHR inversion bit 7. Do not combine this with a PRG/CHR layout that requires those bits to remain set. Switching during rendering changes subsequent pattern fetches. The sample checks with rendering off and restores the font banks before displaying results.

These three intrinsics support CNROM and MMC3. Other boards are rejected at compilation. SUROM also uses CHR control for outer PRG selection and does not allow these CHR operations.

Usage example

c
__chr_bank_set0(4);
    mapper_result[3] = mapper_read(0x03FF);
    mapper_result[4] = mapper_read(0x07FF);

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

The MMC3 sample displays CHR markers 19/20, 21/22 and 23/24. CIRAM reads show A B A B for vertical mirroring and A A B B for horizontal mirroring. IRQ counts are 01→02→03→03: each of the first three explicit enables permits one interrupt; the count stays unchanged after disable. Each stage waits six frames.

    __chr_bank_set0(1); chr_result[1]=chr_marker();
    __chr_bank_set1(3); chr_result[2]=chr_marker();

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

The CNROM lesson shows markers 33, 25 and 41 after SET 2, SET0 1 and SET1 3. It reads original marker bytes through the PPU to demonstrate that all three names switch the entire 8 KiB pattern region.

__copy16

Copy exactly 16 bytes from src to dst, with no length argument. For example, copy one 16-byte record or one Game Boy/NES tile stored in CPU-accessible memory. The number 16 means bytes, not bits; this call does not upload graphics to the display.

Syntax

c
void __copy16(u8* dst, const u8* src);

Parameters

dst

Pointer to the first writable destination byte. Reserve enough consecutive bytes for the complete operation; no buffer is allocated for you.

src

Pointer to the first readable source byte. The entire range must remain accessible and unchanged throughout the copy.

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

Use separate, non-overlapping source and destination ranges. These routines copy forward and do not provide overlap-safe memmove behavior; writing into the unread part of the source can corrupt later bytes.

The operation finishes before the caller continues. It neither switches ROM/RAM banks nor clips a range to a buffer boundary. Keep mappings stable, use valid memory ranges and coordinate access with interrupt handlers that use the same buffers.

On FC, dst is a CPU address, not a PPU address. Copying to CPU RAM does not update CHR, nametables or palettes; use PPU/VRAM APIs to upload that data. Generated helpers share argument/scratch storage, so do not re-enter them from NMI/IRQ while another call is in progress.

Usage example

c
memory_reset();
__copy16(memory_destination+1,memory_source+1);
memory_copy_16=memory_check(16,0); // Exactly 16 bytes, not 16 bits.

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

This example uses __copy16 to copy 16 patterned bytes starting at offset 1. memory_check compares the entire source and destination arrays; the COPY16 row must show 016. Starting inside the buffer leaves a leading guard byte, and bytes after the payload must also remain unchanged.

The complete program resets two 264-byte buffers before each operation, then checks every source byte, every destination byte and the untouched guard regions. The expected rows are COPY WORD 257, FILL WORD 257, COPY BYTE 255, FILL BYTE 255, COPY16 016, COPY32 032, ZERO CALLS 002 and FAILED 000. WORD/BYTE describe the count width, not the size of each copied item. The numbers are produced by the sample's checks, not return values from these void functions.

The captured screens show black lettering on white for DMG, blue on white for CGB and blue on black for FC. This example verifies RAM operations; the lettering presents the results rather than demonstrating a drawing primitive. Separate emulator checks cover 88 memory cases on each platform, including constant and runtime lengths at 0, 1, 16, 17, 32, 33, 64, 65 and 255 bytes, plus 256 and 257 for the word-count forms. Physical hardware has not been tested.

case "__copy16":
                    if (!Need(2)) return true;
                    EmitFixedMemcpy(args[0], args[1], 16, ctx); return true;

void EmitFixedMemcpy(Expr dstExpr, Expr srcExpr, int len, FunctionContext ctx)
        {
            int[] ptr = AcquireTemps(4);
            try
            {
                EmitLoadValue(dstExpr, ctx, 2);
                EmitAsm("STA", Mem(ptr[0]));
                EmitAsm("STX", Mem(ptr[1]));
                EmitLoadValue(srcExpr, ctx, 2);
                EmitAsm("STA", Mem(ptr[2]));
                EmitAsm("STX", Mem(ptr[3]));
                for (int i = 0; i < len; i++)
                {
                    EmitAsm("LDY", Imm(i));
                    EmitAsm("LDA", IndY(ptr[2]));
                    EmitAsm("STA", IndY(ptr[0]));
                }
            }
            finally { ReleaseTemps(ptr); }
        }

            {
                paramTypes = ctx.FindFuncParams(__fname);
                if (paramTypes == null)
                {
                    CType fnTypeFromName;
                    if (TryGetCallableFunctionType(ctx.FindTypeOfName(__fname), out fnTypeFromName))
                        paramTypes = fnTypeFromName.ParamTypes;
                }
            }
            else
            {
                CType fnTypeFromExpr;
                if (TryGetCallableFunctionType(InferType(ctx, newFunc), out fnTypeFromExpr))
                    paramTypes = fnTypeFromExpr.ParamTypes;
            }

            Expr[] newArgs = new Expr[callArgs.Length];
            for (int i = 0; i < callArgs.Length; i++)
            {
                Expr a = LowerExpr(ctx, callArgs[i], allowExtract, prefix);

                bool preserveConstantArgIntrinsic = false;
                if (a.MatchAny(Tag.Call, out Expr argFunc, out Expr[] _argCallArgs) &&
                    argFunc.Match(Tag.Name, out string argFuncName))
                {
                    preserveConstantArgIntrinsic = (argFuncName == "__bankof" || argFuncName == "__cgb_is_cgb");
                }
                // Keep evaluable constants and special intrinsic/bank operands visible to code generation instead of spilling them.
                bool preserveCompileTimeConstantArg = ctx.Global.TryEvalConstInt(a, out _);
                bool preserveFarcallBankArg = (__fname == "__farcall" && i == 0);

                if (allowExtract && !preserveFarcallBankArg && !preserveConstantArgIntrinsic && !preserveCompileTimeConstantArg && !IsAtom(a))
                {
                    // If we know the callee's parameter type, use it to choose a smaller temp.
                    // Example: (u8)(row*32) passed to a u8 param should spill as u8, not u16.
                    CType spillAs = null;
                    if (paramTypes != null && i < paramTypes.Length)
                    {
                        CType pt = paramTypes[i];
                        if (IsU8Like(pt)) spillAs = CType.UInt8;
                    }
                    if (spillAs == null) spillAs = InferType(ctx, a);
                    if (!IsAggregateType(spillAs) && SizeOfType(spillAs) <= 2)

                newArgs[i] = a;

            if (!ctx.InUnsafe && paramTypes != null)
            {
                for (int i = 0; i < newArgs.Length && i < paramTypes.Length; i++)
                {
                    CType pt = paramTypes[i];
                    if (pt == null) continue;
                    if (!IsPointerToNonConst(pt)) continue;
                    if (HasTopLevelCast(newArgs[i])) continue;

                    CType at = InferType(ctx, newArgs[i]);
                    if (at != null && (IsPointerToConst(at) || IsArrayOfConst(at)))
                    {
                        string fn = __fname ?? "<call>";

                        break; // keep it quiet: one warning per call is enough
                    }
                }
            }

            if (paramTypes != null)
            {
                string fn = __fname ?? "<call>";
                for (int i = 0; i < newArgs.Length && i < paramTypes.Length; i++)

                    FilePosition argPos = newArgs[i].Source;

                }
            }

            // Lint: __enum_strict argument passing.
            if (paramTypes != null)
            {
                string fn = __fname ?? "<call>";
                for (int i = 0; i < newArgs.Length && i < paramTypes.Length; i++)
                {
                    CType pt = paramTypes[i];
                    if (pt == null) continue;

                    CType at = InferType(ctx, newArgs[i]);
                    if (at == null) continue;

                    if (HasTopLevelCast(newArgs[i])) continue;

                    if (IsStrictEnum(pt))
                    {
                        if (!IsSameEnum(pt, at))
                        {
                            Program.Warning(expr.Source, ErrorCode.EnumStrictMix,
                                "argument {0} to '{1}' expects __enum_strict {2}, got {3}; cast explicitly to silence",
                                i, fn, pt.Show(), at.Show());
                        }
                    }
                    else if (IsPlainInteger(pt) && IsStrictEnum(at))
                    {
                        Program.Warning(expr.Source, ErrorCode.EnumStrictMix,
                            "argument {0} to '{1}' passes __enum_strict {2} to integer parameter {3}; cast explicitly to silence",
                            i, fn, at.Show(), pt.Show());
                    }
                }
            }

            if (!ctx.InUnsafe)
                RestrictAliasLint(ctx, newFunc, newArgs, expr.Source);

            // __slice(ptr,len) helper: represent a "slice" (ptr+len) in the IR.
            // Semantics: evaluate both arguments, result type is the pointer/array (same as arg0).
            // Bounds checks are injected only with -Zcheck (see Program.CheckSliceBounds).
            // Note: keep the intrinsic name conservative to avoid collisions ("slice" is allowed only
            // when there is no declared function named "slice").
            if (newFunc.Match(Tag.Name, out string __sfname))
            {
                bool isSliceIntrinsic = (__sfname == "__slice") || (__sfname == "slice" && ctx.FindFuncParams("slice") == null);
                if (isSliceIntrinsic)
                {
                    if (newArgs.Length != 2)
                    {
                        Program.Error(expr.Source, ErrorCode.ParseError, "{0}: expected 2 arguments: __slice(ptr,len)", __sfname);
                    }
                    else
                    {
                        CType pty = InferType(ctx, newArgs[0]);
                        if (pty == null || !(pty.IsPointer || pty.IsArray))
                            Program.Error(expr.Source, ErrorCode.ExpectedType, "{0}: first argument must be a pointer or array, got: {1}", __sfname, (pty == null ? "<unknown>" : pty.Show()));

                        CType lty = InferType(ctx, newArgs[1]);
                        if (lty == null || !lty.IsInteger)
                            Program.Error(expr.Source, ErrorCode.ExpectedType, "{0}: second argument must be an integer length, got: {1}", __sfname, (lty == null ? "<unknown>" : lty.Show()));
                    }

                    return Expr.Make(Tag.Slice, newArgs[0], newArgs[1]).WithSource(expr.Source);
                }
            }

            return MakeCall(newFunc, newArgs).WithSource(expr.Source);

Return value

None (void).

        {
            int[] ptr = AcquireTemps(4);

                    WarnImplicitNarrowingIfNeeded(ctx, newArgs[i], InferType(ctx, newArgs[i]), paramTypes[i], argPos,
                        "argument " + i + " to '" + fn + "'");
                }
            }

            // Lint: __enum_strict argument passing.
            if (paramTypes != null)
            {
                string fn = __fname ?? "<call>";
                for (int i = 0; i < newArgs.Length && i < paramTypes.Length; i++)
                {
                    CType pt = paramTypes[i];
                    if (pt == null) continue;

                    CType at = InferType(ctx, newArgs[i]);
                    if (at == null) continue;

                    if (HasTopLevelCast(newArgs[i])) continue;

                    if (IsStrictEnum(pt))
                    {
                        if (!IsSameEnum(pt, at))
                        {
                            Program.Warning(expr.Source, ErrorCode.EnumStrictMix,
                                "argument {0} to '{1}' expects __enum_strict {2}, got {3}; cast explicitly to silence",
                                i, fn, pt.Show(), at.Show());
                        }
                    }
                    else if (IsPlainInteger(pt) && IsStrictEnum(at))
                    {
                        Program.Warning(expr.Source, ErrorCode.EnumStrictMix,
                            "argument {0} to '{1}' passes __enum_strict {2} to integer parameter {3}; cast explicitly to silence",
                            i, fn, at.Show(), pt.Show());
                    }
                }
            }

            if (!ctx.InUnsafe)
                RestrictAliasLint(ctx, newFunc, newArgs, expr.Source);

            // __slice(ptr,len) helper: represent a "slice" (ptr+len) in the IR.
            // Semantics: evaluate both arguments, result type is the pointer/array (same as arg0).
            // Bounds checks are injected only with -Zcheck (see Program.CheckSliceBounds).
            // Note: keep the intrinsic name conservative to avoid collisions ("slice" is allowed only
            // when there is no declared function named "slice").
            if (newFunc.Match(Tag.Name, out string __sfname))
            {
                bool isSliceIntrinsic = (__sfname == "__slice") || (__sfname == "slice" && ctx.FindFuncParams("slice") == null);
                if (isSliceIntrinsic)
                {
                    if (newArgs.Length != 2)
                    {
                        Program.Error(expr.Source, ErrorCode.ParseError, "{0}: expected 2 arguments: __slice(ptr,len)", __sfname);
                    }
                    else
                    {
                        CType pty = InferType(ctx, newArgs[0]);
                        if (pty == null || !(pty.IsPointer || pty.IsArray))
                            Program.Error(expr.Source, ErrorCode.ExpectedType, "{0}: first argument must be a pointer or array, got: {1}", __sfname, (pty == null ? "<unknown>" : pty.Show()));

                        CType lty = InferType(ctx, newArgs[1]);
                        if (lty == null || !lty.IsInteger)
                            Program.Error(expr.Source, ErrorCode.ExpectedType, "{0}: second argument must be an integer length, got: {1}", __sfname, (lty == null ? "<unknown>" : lty.Show()));
                    }

                    return Expr.Make(Tag.Slice, newArgs[0], newArgs[1]).WithSource(expr.Source);
                }
            }

            return MakeCall(newFunc, newArgs).WithSource(expr.Source);
        }
__dot2_q8_8

Compute a unsigned two-term dot product.

Syntax

c
u16 __dot2_q8_8(u16 a0, u16 a1, u8 b0, u8 b1);

Parameters

a0

Unsigned word, 0..65535.

a1

Unsigned word, 0..65535.

b0

Unsigned coefficient, 0..255.

b1

Unsigned coefficient, 0..255.

Return value

Returns the low 16 bits of a0*b0+a1*b1.

Conditions and limits

On FC, q8_8/q1_7 names still use raw integer products without a fixed-point downshift. The Q1.7 functions alias their corresponding signed operations. The caller handles units; signed results are returned as u16 bit patterns.

Usage example

c
// Compare literal coefficients with values read from RAM.
result[22]=__dot2_q8_8(513,769,64,127);
v0=513;v1=769;v2=64;v3=127;
result[23]=__dot2_q8_8(v0,v1,v2,v3);

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

Compare literal inputs with values stored in RAM. Representative results appear as unsigned 16-bit values; negatives use two’s-complement bit patterns. GB rescales fixed-point products, while FC returns integer products, so identical inputs need not give identical results.

The excerpt stores these 16-bit values: result[22]=64959, result[23]=64959. Each literal-input calculation matches its RAM-input counterpart. The screen shows representative values; the result array holds every result.

powershell

__exp_pad_read1

__exp_pad_read1 calls exactly the same compiler helper as __pad_read1_d1. It reads the expansion D1 signal at $4016 with the same latch sequence, eight-bit result and side effects. This name identifies the expansion-input purpose; it does not enable another device mode or combine D0 and D1.

Syntax

c
u8 __exp_pad_read1(void);

Return value

An 8-bit held-button mask in NES raw order. Each set bit identifies a pressed button; 0 means none. It is not a normalized Boolean.

Conditions and limits

NES raw layout: A=0x01, B=0x02, SELECT=0x04, START=0x08, UP=0x10, DOWN=0x20, LEFT=0x40, RIGHT=0x80. A set bit means pressed. Use these values with nes_pad_* and raw __pad_* results, not the shared BTN_* masks from input.h.

Use a peripheral that supplies a compatible eight-bit serial pad stream on the selected D1 line. The function does not detect the attached device or implement every expansion-device protocol. Each call strobes both controller streams; finish a complete read before starting another. Results are fresh snapshots and do not update the input_* or nes_pad1_* caches.

The published KUROSAKI controller model returns only D0 plus fixed bit 6. D1 and the microphone bit are therefore always 0 in that emulator, even while ordinary controller buttons are held. The supplied run verifies compilation, ordinary-button input and this zero-signal observation. Nonzero peripheral signals, electrical timing and real-device compatibility remain unverified; a zero here is not proof that an attached device works or that these functions cannot read it on hardware.

Usage example

c
expansion_first=__exp_pad_read1(); // Same helper as __pad_read1_d1.

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

This program contrasts ordinary D0 input with expansion D1 and the microphone's digital level. Hold A on controller 1 and B on controller 2 until the snapshot is captured. NORMAL P1 and NORMAL P2 display 001 and 002. In the supplied KUROSAKI run, D1 PORT 1, D1 PORT 2, EXP ALIAS 1, EXP ALIAS 2, MIC LEVEL and MIC DIRECT all display 000 because those signal lines are not emulated. The displayed values then stay fixed. With suitable peripherals and an implementation of their signal lines, the expansion and microphone values depend on the actual inputs; consult the bit layouts above rather than expecting these zeros.

The published KUROSAKI controller model returns only D0 plus fixed bit 6. D1 and the microphone bit are therefore always 0 in that emulator, even while ordinary controller buttons are held. The supplied run verifies compilation, ordinary-button input and this zero-signal observation. Nonzero peripheral signals, electrical timing and real-device compatibility remain unverified; a zero here is not proof that an attached device works or that these functions cannot read it on hardware.

__far_memcpy

Temporarily select a ROM bank, copy len bytes from src to dst in increasing address order, then restore the compiler’s saved ROM bank. __farmemcpy and __far_memcpy use the same implementation on this platform.

Syntax

c
void __far_memcpy(u8* dst, u8 bank, u16 src, u16 len);

Parameters

dst

Destination in writable memory. Reserve enough space for every byte copied. Except for a zero-byte transfer, a null or invalid destination is not checked.

bank

8-bit bank selector for the source ROM mapping. Use a bank supported by the cartridge and the compiler’s bank layout; this argument is separate from the source address.

src

16-bit CPU address of source bytes in the selected ROM mapping. The FC declaration takes u16; cast a resource pointer with (u16)pointer.

len

Byte count, 0–65535. Zero performs no memory copy, but the bank-selection and restoration steps still run.

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

Keep the full source range in the intended ROM mapping and the full destination range in writable memory. Copying does not select the next bank at a window boundary, handle overlapping ranges like memmove, or provide VRAM-safe writes. Use the graphics transfer APIs for VRAM.

The samples place calling code in fixed bank 0 so source-bank changes cannot unmap the code being executed. These transfers are synchronous. Do not interrupt a transfer with another bank-changing copy or assume the helper makes a whole application interrupt-safe.

Usage example

c
__far_memcpy(buffer,payload_bank,(u16)payload_pointer,32);
expect(*asset_bank_marker==0xA1 && bank_get_current()==1,27);
for(i=0;i<32;i++) expect(buffer[(__safe_index u8)i]==expected_shape_byte(i),28);
buffer[32]=0x55;
__far_memcpy(buffer+32,2,(u16)asset_shapes,0);
expect(buffer[32]==0x55 && *asset_bank_marker==0xA1,30);

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

Copy two patterns, 32 bytes, from payload bank 2 while bank 1 is initially selected. The program compares every copied byte, checks that bank 1 is restored and verifies that a zero-length copy leaves a 0x55 sentinel unchanged.

Expected image: a red row starts at pixel (16,32) and spans 72×8 pixels. It repeats an 8×8 triangle, an 8×8 square outline with a one-pixel border, and a tile with its left four columns filled, three times. The triangle grows from one pixel at the top left to eight pixels on its bottom row.

On FC, a blue triangle and outline at (16,64) show __far_memcpy; a green pair at (16,96) shows asset_load_raw followed by a CHR upload. Each pair occupies 16×8 pixels on a black background. These rows demonstrate copied image bytes, not merely numeric status values.

Expected status: FAILED CHECKS 000 and FIRST FAILURE 00. The verification runs 300 frames and compares text, shape masks and colors against these expectations. This is emulator evidence, not a physical-hardware test.

__farcall

Call a named function with no arguments. The FC compiler uses the function's assigned bank to choose a direct call or a bank-restoring helper. It evaluates the bank argument, but the target's placement determines the selected bank.

Syntax

c
__farcall(bank, function_name);

Parameters

bank

An unsigned 8-bit ROM-bank number. For a call, it must agree with the function's placement; for a read, it selects the source mapping. Use the target cartridge's valid range.

func

The declared name of a function with no parameters. A variable holding a function address is not accepted by this named-call intrinsic. The bank argument is not forwarded as a callback parameter.

Return value

The called function's result type determines the result. A void callback yields no value; u8 and u16 callbacks return their scalar value. The displayed sample uses void callbacks.

Conditions and limits

These calls do not forward user arguments or make the callback interrupt-reentrant. Keep the callback's own data, stack and interrupt use valid. The bank-restoring call paths are tested with nested calls and repeated calls; physical hardware and arbitrary interrupt interleavings are not covered by this example.

FC switch-bank numbers are logical compiler numbers. Zero denotes common ROM, not a switch target. The helper normalizes zero to bank 1. On SUROM512, only 1–30 are valid: an out-of-range constant passed directly to the switching intrinsic is a build error; an invalid runtime value falls back to 1 and sets the mapper-fault state. Read common ROM directly instead of requesting a bank-zero switch.

Usage example

c
__farcall(3,callback);
bank_expect(callback_count==2 && callback_byte==0xD3,16);

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

At this point in the complete program, __farcall raises callback_count to 2. The callback reads D3 from bank 3. A later near read of B2 from home2 verifies that execution returned with bank 2 mapped.

The complete program teaches how a bank number and near address identify data, how callbacks cross banks, and how to distinguish the library's record from the actual mapping. All displayed numbers are hexadecimal. BANK IN and BANK OUT must show 02, BYTE HEX D3, WORD HEX 5C7A, and both FAILED CHECKS and FIRST FAILURE 00. CGB and FC display blue text; DMG displays black text.

CALL COUNT is 02: the far_call macro and __farcall each invoke the callback once.

if (string.Equals(funcName, "__farcall", StringComparison.Ordinal))
            {
                Expr[] farArgs = args ?? Array.Empty<Expr>();
                if (farArgs.Length != 2)
                {
                    Program.Error("error KQ0000: __farcall(bank, func) expects exactly 2 arguments.");
                    return;
                }

                string targetName;
                if (!farArgs[1].Match(Tag.Name, out targetName))
                {
                    Program.Error("error KQ0000: __farcall(bank, func) requires the 2nd argument to be a function name.");
                    return;
                }
                // This intrinsic supplies no callback arguments. A variable name
                // is not a static function target, even when its value is a pointer.
                if (!_functionParameters.TryGetValue(targetName, out FieldInfo[] farParameters))
                {
                    Program.Error("error KQFC2610: __farcall requires a declared function name; use an ordinary typed call for a function pointer.");
                    return;
                }
                if (farParameters.Length != 0)
                {
                    Program.Error("error KQFC2610: __farcall requires a callback with no parameters.");
                    return;
                }
                if (Program.NesMapperProfile.IsSurom512 &&
                    TryEvaluateConstant(farArgs[0], out int constantFarBank) &&
                    (constantFarBank < 1 || constantFarBank > 30))
                {
                    Program.Error("error KQFC2603 KQFC-SUROM-BANK-RANGE: __farcall constant bank {0} is outside 1..30; common bank 0 is not a switch target.", constantFarBank);
                    return;
                }

                // Evaluate the requested far-call bank byte; the following dispatch uses the target function bank metadata.
                EmitLoadValue(farArgs[0], ctx, 1);

                int callerBank = ctx == null ? 0 : ctx.Bank;
                int calleeBank = GetFunctionBank(targetName);
                if (ShouldUseFdsOverlayThunk(callerBank, calleeBank))
                {
                    string fdsThunkName = EnsureFdsOverlayThunk(targetName, calleeBank);
                    EmitAsm("JSR", Abs(fdsThunkName));
                    RecordCallEdge(targetName, calleeBank, "fds_overlay_thunk", viaThunk: true, viaFarcall: true);
                    return;
                }
                bool bankedPrg = Program.NesMapperProfile.SupportsPrgBanking || Program.NesMapperProfile.UsesDuplicatedCommonBank;
                bool directSafe = !bankedPrg || calleeBank == 0 || calleeBank == callerBank;
                if (directSafe)
                {
                    EmitAsm("JSR", Abs(targetName));
                    RecordCallEdge(targetName, calleeBank, "direct", viaThunk: false, viaFarcall: true);
                    return;
                }

                string thunkName = EnsureBankThunk(targetName, calleeBank);
                EmitAsm("JSR", Abs(thunkName));
                RecordCallEdge(targetName, calleeBank, "bank_thunk", viaThunk: true, viaFarcall: true);
                return;
            }
__farpeek16

Read a little-endian 16-bit value at addr and addr+1 under a temporary bank selection, then restore the bank. This is the intrinsic used by far_data_read16.

Syntax

c
u16 __farpeek16(u8 bank, u16 addr);

Parameters

bank

An unsigned 8-bit ROM-bank number. For a call, it must agree with the function's placement; for a read, it selects the source mapping. Use the target cartridge's valid range.

addr

16-bit CPU address of source bytes in the selected ROM mapping. The FC declaration takes u16; cast a resource pointer with (u16)pointer.

Return value

The little-endian word read, as u16 (0–65535).

Conditions and limits

The complete byte or word must be readable in the selected CPU mapping. These reads do not validate pointers, clip addresses or advance automatically to another ROM bank at a window boundary. A word read needs two valid consecutive bytes.

Far reads and copies are synchronous and use shared compiler scratch. Do not let an interrupt run another banked transfer over the same scratch while one is active. On GB, the copy helper also uses one shared HRAM slot for the saved bank. The sample performs these operations from fixed code with no competing banked-transfer handler.

FC switch-bank numbers are logical compiler numbers. Zero denotes common ROM, not a switch target. The helper normalizes zero to bank 1. On SUROM512, only 1–30 are valid: an out-of-range constant passed directly to the switching intrinsic is a build error; an invalid runtime value falls back to 1 and sets the mapper-fault state. Read common ROM directly instead of requesting a bank-zero switch.

Usage example

c
bank_expect(__farpeek16(3,(u16)(payload+1))==0x5C7A,14);

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

This excerpt uses __farpeek16 to read payload+1 in bank 3 and checks 5C7A. In the full program, the near read from home2 also confirms that the bank-2 mapping is restored.

The complete program teaches how a bank number and near address identify data, how callbacks cross banks, and how to distinguish the library's record from the actual mapping. All displayed numbers are hexadecimal. BANK IN and BANK OUT must show 02, BYTE HEX D3, WORD HEX 5C7A, and both FAILED CHECKS and FIRST FAILURE 00. CGB and FC display blue text; DMG displays black text.

CALL COUNT is 02: the far_call macro and __farcall each invoke the callback once.

__fkb_detect

Probe the keyboard detection pattern before interpreting key presses.

Syntax

c
u8 __fkb_detect(void);

Return value

Returns 1 if row 9, column 0 reads 0x1E and the disabled matrix reads zero; otherwise 0. This is a signal-pattern heuristic, not a device identification code.

Conditions and limits

These APIs access $4016/$4017 directly. Do not interleave interrupt-driven gamepad, keyboard or serial operations on the same ports. Controller shift positions can also be affected. The sample disables NMI while capturing input, then enables it when initializing the display.

Writes 5 to $4016 to reset row 0, then advances rows using high-to-low transitions of the column-select bit. The generated code includes 12 CPU cycles of NOPs after reset and 50 after column selection, in addition to surrounding instructions. It writes zero on exit to disable the matrix.

A separate regression checks rows 0..9, both columns, the nine-row scan, settling delays and final port state from executed CPU bus traces. It does not inject physical key signals.

Row 9 has no keys. A failed condition returns zero immediately. KUROSAKI returns zero on the first read, so detection fails there.

These images run the downloadable ROMs unchanged in KUROSAKI. Its current input bus models gamepads but not keyboard, light-gun or serial-adapter signals. The external input bits read as zero, so the captures do not verify those devices. Physical key input, optical sensing and communication remain untested.

NESdev: Family BASIC Keyboard

Usage example

c
#include "fc_ports_scene.h"
void main(void){
    u8 row;
    __irq_disable();__ppu_ctrl_set(0);port_phase=1;
    port_result[0]=__fkb_detect();
    __fkb_scan(key_matrix);
    port_result[1]=__fkb_read_row_col(6,0);
    port_result[2]=0;
    if(port_result[0] && !(port_result[1]&16))port_result[2]=1;
    port_phase=2;port_result[31]=165;
    m_init();m_text(2,2,"KEYBOARD STARTUP SNAPSHOT");m_wait();
    m_text(2,4,"DEVICE DETECT");port_number(25,4,port_result[0]);m_wait();
    m_text(2,6,"ROW 6 COL 0");port_number(25,6,port_result[1]);m_wait();
    m_text(2,8,"A KEY - GUARDED");port_number(25,8,port_result[2]);m_wait();
    m_text(2,10,"ROW   COL0  COL1  (HEX)");m_wait();
    for(row=0;row<9;row++){
        m_put(3,12+row,'0'+row);port_hex(9,12+row,key_matrix[row*2]);port_hex(15,12+row,key_matrix[row*2+1]);m_wait();
    }
    m_text(2,23,"RAW MATRIX - NOT ASCII");m_wait();
    while(1){m_wait();}
}

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

In this KUROSAKI run, DEVICE DETECT, ROW 6 COL 0 and A KEY - GUARDED are all 000; all nine COL0/COL1 pairs are 00. A is row 6, column 0, bit 4, but failed detection prevents the raw zero from being reported as a key press. The table is a single startup capture.

__fkb_read_row_col

Read one selected row and column group without an 18-byte buffer when only a particular group is needed.

Syntax

c
u8 __fkb_read_row_col(u8 row, u8 col);

Parameters

row

Use 0..8 for key rows or 9 for the keyless detection row. No runtime range check is generated.

col

0 or 1. Only the low bit is used: even values select group 0 and odd values group 1.

Return value

Returns $4017 & 0x1E without packing the bits down.

Conditions and limits

These APIs access $4016/$4017 directly. Do not interleave interrupt-driven gamepad, keyboard or serial operations on the same ports. Controller shift positions can also be affected. The sample disables NMI while capturing input, then enables it when initializing the display.

Key groups are raw bits 1..4: a pressed key clears its bit, and an idle group is 0x1E. They are neither ASCII text nor a bitmap with one meaning pressed. A disconnected device can also read zero; do not interpret that as every key being held without checking presence.

Writes 5 to $4016 to reset row 0, then advances rows using high-to-low transitions of the column-select bit. The generated code includes 12 CPU cycles of NOPs after reset and 50 after column selection, in addition to surrounding instructions. It writes zero on exit to disable the matrix.

A separate regression checks rows 0..9, both columns, the nine-row scan, settling delays and final port state from executed CPU bus traces. It does not inject physical key signals.

Resets to row 0 and advances afresh for every call; it does not reuse the previous call’s row position.

These images run the downloadable ROMs unchanged in KUROSAKI. Its current input bus models gamepads but not keyboard, light-gun or serial-adapter signals. The external input bits read as zero, so the captures do not verify those devices. Physical key input, optical sensing and communication remain untested.

Conditions and limits

These APIs access $4016/$4017 directly. Do not interleave interrupt-driven gamepad, keyboard or serial operations on the same ports. Controller shift positions can also be affected. The sample disables NMI while capturing input, then enables it when initializing the display.

Key groups are raw bits 1..4: a pressed key clears its bit, and an idle group is 0x1E. They are neither ASCII text nor a bitmap with one meaning pressed. A disconnected device can also read zero; do not interpret that as every key being held without checking presence.

Writes 5 to $4016 to reset row 0, then advances rows using high-to-low transitions of the column-select bit. The generated code includes 12 CPU cycles of NOPs after reset and 50 after column selection, in addition to surrounding instructions. It writes zero on exit to disable the matrix.

A separate regression checks rows 0..9, both columns, the nine-row scan, settling delays and final port state from executed CPU bus traces. It does not inject physical key signals.

Reads column 0 then column 1 for each row. This is sequential scanning, not a simultaneous snapshot of every key. A zero-valued group does not terminate the scan early.

These images run the downloadable ROMs unchanged in KUROSAKI. Its current input bus models gamepads but not keyboard, light-gun or serial-adapter signals. The external input bits read as zero, so the captures do not verify those devices. Physical key input, optical sensing and communication remain untested.

NESdev: Family BASIC Keyboard

Usage example

c
#include "fc_ports_scene.h"
void main(void){
    u8 row;
    __irq_disable();__ppu_ctrl_set(0);port_phase=1;
    port_result[0]=__fkb_detect();
    __fkb_scan(key_matrix);
    port_result[1]=__fkb_read_row_col(6,0);
    port_result[2]=0;
    if(port_result[0] && !(port_result[1]&16))port_result[2]=1;
    port_phase=2;port_result[31]=165;
    m_init();m_text(2,2,"KEYBOARD STARTUP SNAPSHOT");m_wait();
    m_text(2,4,"DEVICE DETECT");port_number(25,4,port_result[0]);m_wait();
    m_text(2,6,"ROW 6 COL 0");port_number(25,6,port_result[1]);m_wait();
    m_text(2,8,"A KEY - GUARDED");port_number(25,8,port_result[2]);m_wait();
    m_text(2,10,"ROW   COL0  COL1  (HEX)");m_wait();
    for(row=0;row<9;row++){
        m_put(3,12+row,'0'+row);port_hex(9,12+row,key_matrix[row*2]);port_hex(15,12+row,key_matrix[row*2+1]);m_wait();
    }
    m_text(2,23,"RAW MATRIX - NOT ASCII");m_wait();
    while(1){m_wait();}
}

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

In this KUROSAKI run, DEVICE DETECT, ROW 6 COL 0 and A KEY - GUARDED are all 000; all nine COL0/COL1 pairs are 00. A is row 6, column 0, bit 4, but failed detection prevents the raw zero from being reported as a key press. The table is a single startup capture.

__irq_disable

Emit SEI to set the CPU status register's I bit and mask ordinary IRQ requests. Use this for an IRQ-critical section. It does not disable NMI, silence the APU, acknowledge an IRQ source or save the previous mask.

Syntax

c
void __irq_disable(void);

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

The I bit only controls ordinary IRQ: NMI can still interrupt this critical section. Masking IRQ neither acknowledges a pending device request nor protects data shared with NMI. Prepare sources and handlers separately. The sample does not test an IRQ-generating peripheral.

NESdev: NMI

NESdev: CPU interrupts

Usage example

c
__irq_disable();
disabled=(__irq_save()&4)>>2; // The CPU I bit must be 1.

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

The program shows how the CPU IRQ mask differs from PPU NMI control. On the black screen, blue text must show IRQ DISABLED I = 001, IRQ ENABLED I = 000, SAVED SECTION I = 001 and RESTORED I = 000. Each value is the extracted I bit, not the whole status byte. FAILED CHECKS must be 000.

Run for at least 360 emulator frames so the 256-wait demonstration can finish. NMI DELTA 3 WAITS must be 003 even with IRQ masked; NMI DELTA 256 WAITS must be 000 because the byte wraps. NMI OFF DELTA must be 000. This program uses the default handler without runtime.c. Separate state checks cover 21 cases, including status-bit restoration and bounded waits with NMI disabled or an empty custom handler. KUROSAKI/NROM is tested; physical hardware is not.

__irq_restore

Evaluate the supplied status byte, push it with PHA and restore CPU status with PLP. This restores the saved IRQ mask and arithmetic flags, rather than always enabling IRQ. Ordinary C expressions executed afterward may change arithmetic flags again.

Syntax

c
void __irq_restore(u8 state);

Parameters

state

The full 8-bit processor-status value captured by __irq_save. Preserve it for __irq_restore; do not convert it to a Boolean. Bit 2 is I: 1 masks IRQ, 0 allows it. PHP's stacked representation sets bits 4 and 5.

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

The I bit only controls ordinary IRQ: NMI can still interrupt this critical section. Masking IRQ neither acknowledges a pending device request nor protects data shared with NMI. Prepare sources and handlers separately. The sample does not test an IRQ-generating peripheral.
