__irq_scanline_set

Alias of the MMC3 latch/reload operation in __mapper_irq_set. The word scanline does not guarantee an absolute screen row.

Syntax

c
void __irq_scanline_set(u8 line);

Parameters

line

An 8-bit counter latch value, 0..255, not an absolute screen Y coordinate. Reload timing and qualified PPU A12 transitions determine when it fires. Zero is valid and does not mean “disable interrupts.”

Return value

No return value.

Conditions and limits

Intrinsic declarations are in intrinsics.h. Include nes_game.h for the nes_mapper_irq_* macros. Select the board at build time with --mapper.

MMC3 only. Supply a __nes_irq handler, qualified PPU A12 transitions, mapper IRQ enable and CPU __irq_enable(). The sample enables rendering with background patterns at $0000 and sprite patterns at $1000. This lesson does not verify synchronization to an exact line on physical hardware.

MMC3 acknowledgment and disable both write $E000. This clears the current request and disables subsequent requests. Call __mapper_irq_enable() again at the intended time to arm another interrupt. Neither operation changes the CPU interrupt mask or NMI enable.

The compiler emits RTI for a custom interrupt handler, but the handler must preserve any A/X/Y registers and shared scratch that it changes. The sample saves A/X/Y and uses only a byte increment and argument-free acknowledgment. If you add C calls, also inspect the shared storage they use.

Usage example

c
irq_phase=2;
    __irq_scanline_set(7); __mapper_irq_enable();
    for (i=0;i<6;i++) { m_wait(); }
    mapper_result[17]=irq_count;

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

The MMC3 sample displays CHR markers 19/20, 21/22 and 23/24. CIRAM reads show A B A B for vertical mirroring and A A B B for horizontal mirroring. IRQ counts are 01→02→03→03: each of the first three explicit enables permits one interrupt; the count stays unchanged after disable. Each stage waits six frames.

__joypad2p_voice

__joypad2p_voice is another entry name for the __mic_read2p helper. Both read the same digital microphone bit. The word “voice” does not imply audio processing; separate calls take separate samples and can differ if the signal changes between them.

Read the digital signal for the second Famicom controller's microphone from $4016 bit 2. The helper reads the register once, masks 0x04 and normalizes the result to 0 or 1 without inversion. It does not latch controllers, record audio, measure volume or recognize speech.

Syntax

c
u8 __joypad2p_voice(void);

Return value

Exactly 1 when $4016 & 0x04 is nonzero, otherwise 0. This is the sampled digital level, not a button mask, amplitude, frequency or count of spoken words.

Conditions and limits

Although the microphone belongs to controller 2, this helper accesses $4016, not $4017. A register read can also advance the controller's serial stream while strobe is low, so do not insert microphone reads inside another controller's eight-bit read loop. No input-history cache is updated.

The published KUROSAKI controller model returns only D0 plus fixed bit 6. D1 and the microphone bit are therefore always 0 in that emulator, even while ordinary controller buttons are held. The supplied run verifies compilation, ordinary-button input and this zero-signal observation. Nonzero peripheral signals, electrical timing and real-device compatibility remain unverified; a zero here is not proof that an attached device works or that these functions cannot read it on hardware.

Usage example

c
voice=__joypad2p_voice();

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

This program contrasts ordinary D0 input with expansion D1 and the microphone's digital level. Hold A on controller 1 and B on controller 2 until the snapshot is captured. NORMAL P1 and NORMAL P2 display 001 and 002. In the supplied KUROSAKI run, D1 PORT 1, D1 PORT 2, EXP ALIAS 1, EXP ALIAS 2, MIC LEVEL and MIC DIRECT all display 000 because those signal lines are not emulated. The displayed values then stay fixed. With suitable peripherals and an implementation of their signal lines, the expansion and microphone values depend on the actual inputs; consult the bit layouts above rather than expecting these zeros.

__mac16

Compute a unsigned multiply-accumulate.

Syntax

c
u16 __mac16(u16 acc, u16 a, u8 b);

Parameters

acc

16-bit accumulator to add.

a

Unsigned word, 0..65535.

b

Unsigned coefficient, 0..255.

Return value

Returns the low 16 bits of acc+a*b.

Conditions and limits

On FC, q8_8/q1_7 names still use raw integer products without a fixed-point downshift. The Q1.7 functions alias their corresponding signed operations. The caller handles units; signed results are returned as u16 bit patterns.

Usage example

c
// Compare literal coefficients with values read from RAM.
result[8]=__mac16(65500,513,127);
v0=65500;v1=513;v2=127;
result[9]=__mac16(v0,v1,v2);

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

Compare literal inputs with values stored in RAM. Representative results appear as unsigned 16-bit values; negatives use two’s-complement bit patterns. GB rescales fixed-point products, while FC returns integer products, so identical inputs need not give identical results.

The excerpt stores these 16-bit values: result[8]=65115, result[9]=65115. Each literal-input calculation matches its RAM-input counterpart. The screen shows representative values; the result array holds every result.

__mapper_id

Return the mapper number selected at build time, for board-specific initialization or display.

Syntax

c
u8 __mapper_id(void);

Return value

An 8-bit mapper number: NROM=0, MMC1=1, UxROM=2, CNROM=3, MMC3=4, MMC5=5, AxROM=7, VRC6=24, FME7=69 and VRC7=85. The compiler emits a constant; this does not probe the running hardware.

Conditions and limits

Intrinsic declarations are in intrinsics.h. Include nes_game.h for the nes_mapper_irq_* macros. Select the board at build time with --mapper.

Usage example

c
mapper_result[0] = __mapper_id();

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

The MMC3 sample displays CHR markers 19/20, 21/22 and 23/24. CIRAM reads show A B A B for vertical mirroring and A A B B for horizontal mirroring. IRQ counts are 01→02→03→03: each of the first three explicit enables permits one interrupt; the count stays unchanged after disable. Each stage waits six frames.

Complete example program

Build command

powershell
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force .\out | Out-Null
.\kitaqfc\kitaqfc.exe .\kitaq-docs\samples\api-examples\fc\mapper_controls.c -I .\kitaqfc\lib -I .\kitaq-docs\samples -o .\out\mapper_controls.nes --mapper=mmc3 --nes-chr=.\kitaq-docs\samples\mapper_banks.chr --no-cache --no-disasm

__mapper_irq_ack

Acknowledge MMC3 in the IRQ handler. Because this writes $E000, it also disables subsequent IRQ requests.

Syntax

c
void __mapper_irq_ack(void);

Return value

No return value.

Conditions and limits

Intrinsic declarations are in intrinsics.h. Include nes_game.h for the nes_mapper_irq_* macros. Select the board at build time with --mapper.

MMC3 only. Supply a __nes_irq handler, qualified PPU A12 transitions, mapper IRQ enable and CPU __irq_enable(). The sample enables rendering with background patterns at $0000 and sprite patterns at $1000. This lesson does not verify synchronization to an exact line on physical hardware.

MMC3 acknowledgment and disable both write $E000. This clears the current request and disables subsequent requests. Call __mapper_irq_enable() again at the intended time to arm another interrupt. Neither operation changes the CPU interrupt mask or NMI enable.

The compiler emits RTI for a custom interrupt handler, but the handler must preserve any A/X/Y registers and shared scratch that it changes. The sample saves A/X/Y and uses only a byte increment and argument-free acknowledgment. If you add C calls, also inspect the shared storage they use.

Usage example

c
void __nes_irq(void) {
    __asm {
        PHA
        TXA
        PHA
        TYA
        PHA
    }
    irq_count++;
    if (irq_phase == 1) { nes_mapper_irq_ack(); }
    else { __mapper_irq_ack(); }
    __asm {
        PLA
        TAY
        PLA
        TAX
        PLA
    }
}

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

The MMC3 sample displays CHR markers 19/20, 21/22 and 23/24. CIRAM reads show A B A B for vertical mirroring and A A B B for horizontal mirroring. IRQ counts are 01→02→03→03: each of the first three explicit enables permits one interrupt; the count stays unchanged after disable. Each stage waits six frames.

__memcpy

Copy a caller-specified number of bytes from src to dst. The 16-bit count supports transfers longer than 255 bytes, such as copying a complete RAM table. Bytes are read and written in ascending address order.

Syntax

c
void __memcpy(u8* dst, const u8* src, u16 len);

Parameters

dst

Pointer to the first writable destination byte. Reserve enough consecutive bytes for the complete operation; no buffer is allocated for you.

src

Pointer to the first readable source byte. The entire range must remain accessible and unchanged throughout the copy.

len

Number of bytes as u16 (0–65535), not an element count. The type's maximum is not a promise that such a large valid buffer exists on the target machine. Keep the whole range within the selected memory mapping.

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

A zero count transfers no bytes. Side effects in argument expressions still occur: the example calls two pointer-returning functions and observes both calls even though the copy length is zero.

Use separate, non-overlapping source and destination ranges. These routines copy forward and do not provide overlap-safe memmove behavior; writing into the unread part of the source can corrupt later bytes.

The operation finishes before the caller continues. It neither switches ROM/RAM banks nor clips a range to a buffer boundary. Keep mappings stable, use valid memory ranges and coordinate access with interrupt handlers that use the same buffers.

On FC, dst is a CPU address, not a PPU address. Copying to CPU RAM does not update CHR, nametables or palettes; use PPU/VRAM APIs to upload that data. Generated helpers share argument/scratch storage, so do not re-enter them from NMI/IRQ while another call is in progress.

Usage example

c
memory_reset();
__memcpy(memory_destination+1,memory_source+1,257);
memory_copy_word=memory_check(257,0); // 257 copied bytes; guards unchanged.

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

This example uses __memcpy to copy 257 patterned bytes starting at offset 1. memory_check compares the entire source and destination arrays; the COPY WORD row must show 257. Starting inside the buffer leaves a leading guard byte, and bytes after the payload must also remain unchanged.

The complete program resets two 264-byte buffers before each operation, then checks every source byte, every destination byte and the untouched guard regions. The expected rows are COPY WORD 257, FILL WORD 257, COPY BYTE 255, FILL BYTE 255, COPY16 016, COPY32 032, ZERO CALLS 002 and FAILED 000. WORD/BYTE describe the count width, not the size of each copied item. The numbers are produced by the sample's checks, not return values from these void functions.

The captured screens show black lettering on white for DMG, blue on white for CGB and blue on black for FC. This example verifies RAM operations; the lettering presents the results rather than demonstrating a drawing primitive. Separate emulator checks cover 88 memory cases on each platform, including constant and runtime lengths at 0, 1, 16, 17, 32, 33, 64, 65 and 255 bytes, plus 256 and 257 for the word-count forms. Physical hardware has not been tested.

bool TryEmitMemcpyOrMemsetInline(string funcName, Expr[] args, FunctionContext ctx, bool isSet, int lenIndex, int lenSize)
        {
            args = args ?? Array.Empty<Expr>();
            int expected = isSet ? 3 : 3;
            if (args.Length != expected) return false;
            if (!TryEvaluateConstant(args[lenIndex], out int len)) return false;
            if (len < 0 || len > 32) return false;
            int valueConst = 0;
            if (isSet && !TryEvaluateConstant(args[1], out valueConst)) return false;
            // A zero-length expansion emits no address or fill evaluation in this helper.
            if (len == 0) return true;
            if (isSet)
            {
                int[] ptr = AcquireTemps(2);
                try
                {
                    EmitLoadValue(args[0], ctx, 2);
                    EmitAsm("STA", Mem(ptr[0]));
                    EmitAsm("STX", Mem(ptr[1]));
                    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++)
                    {
                        EmitAsm("LDY", Imm(i));
                        EmitAsm("LDA", Imm(valueConst));
                        EmitAsm("STA", IndY(ptr[0]));
                    }
                }
                finally { ReleaseTemps(ptr); }
                return true;
            }
            EmitFixedMemcpy(args[0], args[1], len, ctx);
            return true;
        }

void EmitFixedMemcpy(Expr dstExpr, Expr srcExpr, int len, FunctionContext ctx)
        {
            int[] ptr = AcquireTemps(4);
            try
            {
                EmitLoadValue(dstExpr, ctx, 2);
                EmitAsm("STA", Mem(ptr[0]));
                EmitAsm("STX", Mem(ptr[1]));
                EmitLoadValue(srcExpr, ctx, 2);
                EmitAsm("STA", Mem(ptr[2]));
                EmitAsm("STX", Mem(ptr[3]));
                for (int i = 0; i < len; i++)
                {
                    EmitAsm("LDY", Imm(i));
                    EmitAsm("LDA", IndY(ptr[2]));
                    EmitAsm("STA", IndY(ptr[0]));
                }
            }
            finally { ReleaseTemps(ptr); }
        }

__memcpy_small

Copy a block of at most 255 bytes using an 8-bit count. Use this form when the transfer length fits in a byte. _small describes the count width; it is not a promise of a particular execution time or generated code size.

Syntax

c
void __memcpy_small(u8* dst, const u8* src, u8 len);

Parameters

dst

Pointer to the first writable destination byte. Reserve enough consecutive bytes for the complete operation; no buffer is allocated for you.

src

Pointer to the first readable source byte. The entire range must remain accessible and unchanged throughout the copy.

len

Number of bytes as u8: 0–255. Do not pass 256 to mean a full 256-byte block; that length does not fit this parameter. Use the corresponding function without _small for 256 bytes or more.

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

A zero count transfers no bytes. Side effects in argument expressions still occur: the example calls two pointer-returning functions and observes both calls even though the copy length is zero.

Use separate, non-overlapping source and destination ranges. These routines copy forward and do not provide overlap-safe memmove behavior; writing into the unread part of the source can corrupt later bytes.

The operation finishes before the caller continues. It neither switches ROM/RAM banks nor clips a range to a buffer boundary. Keep mappings stable, use valid memory ranges and coordinate access with interrupt handlers that use the same buffers.

On FC, dst is a CPU address, not a PPU address. Copying to CPU RAM does not update CHR, nametables or palettes; use PPU/VRAM APIs to upload that data. Generated helpers share argument/scratch storage, so do not re-enter them from NMI/IRQ while another call is in progress.

Usage example

c
memory_reset();
__memcpy_small(memory_destination+1,memory_source+1,255);
memory_copy_byte=memory_check(255,0); // Maximum representable byte count.

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

The complete program resets two 264-byte buffers before each operation, then checks every source byte, every destination byte and the untouched guard regions. The expected rows are COPY WORD 257, FILL WORD 257, COPY BYTE 255, FILL BYTE 255, COPY16 016, COPY32 032, ZERO CALLS 002 and FAILED 000. WORD/BYTE describe the count width, not the size of each copied item. The numbers are produced by the sample's checks, not return values from these void functions.

__memset

Write the same byte value throughout a destination range. The 16-bit count is useful for clearing a large buffer or initializing a table. For example, filling with 0x5A writes 5A 5A 5A…; it does not repeat a multibyte integer.

Syntax

c
void __memset(u8* dst, u8 value, u16 len);

Parameters

dst

Pointer to the first writable destination byte. Reserve enough consecutive bytes for the complete operation; no buffer is allocated for you.

value

The byte repeated at every destination address: 0–255. Use 0 to clear the range. To initialize a u16 array to a nonzero numeric value, assign its elements individually instead.

len

Number of bytes as u16 (0–65535), not an element count. The type's maximum is not a promise that such a large valid buffer exists on the target machine. Keep the whole range within the selected memory mapping.

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

A zero count transfers no bytes. Side effects in argument expressions still occur: the example calls two pointer-returning functions and observes both calls even though the copy length is zero.

The operation finishes before the caller continues. It neither switches ROM/RAM banks nor clips a range to a buffer boundary. Keep mappings stable, use valid memory ranges and coordinate access with interrupt handlers that use the same buffers.

On FC, dst is a CPU address, not a PPU address. Copying to CPU RAM does not update CHR, nametables or palettes; use PPU/VRAM APIs to upload that data. Generated helpers share argument/scratch storage, so do not re-enter them from NMI/IRQ while another call is in progress.

Usage example

c
memory_reset();
__memset(memory_destination+1,0x5A,257);
memory_fill_word=memory_check(257,1); // Repeat one byte, not a 16-bit word.

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

This example uses __memset to fill 257 bytes at offset 1 with 0x5A. memory_check requires every byte in that range to equal 0x5A, while the guard bytes stay 0xCC and the separate source buffer remains untouched. The FILL WORD row must show 257.

The complete program resets two 264-byte buffers before each operation, then checks every source byte, every destination byte and the untouched guard regions. The expected rows are COPY WORD 257, FILL WORD 257, COPY BYTE 255, FILL BYTE 255, COPY16 016, COPY32 032, ZERO CALLS 002 and FAILED 000. WORD/BYTE describe the count width, not the size of each copied item. The numbers are produced by the sample's checks, not return values from these void functions.

The captured screens show black lettering on white for DMG, blue on white for CGB and blue on black for FC. This example verifies RAM operations; the lettering presents the results rather than demonstrating a drawing primitive. Separate emulator checks cover 88 memory cases on each platform, including constant and runtime lengths at 0, 1, 16, 17, 32, 33, 64, 65 and 255 bytes, plus 256 and 257 for the word-count forms. Physical hardware has not been tested.

bool TryEmitMemcpyOrMemsetInline(string funcName, Expr[] args, FunctionContext ctx, bool isSet, int lenIndex, int lenSize)
        {
            args = args ?? Array.Empty<Expr>();
            int expected = isSet ? 3 : 3;
            if (args.Length != expected) return false;
            if (!TryEvaluateConstant(args[lenIndex], out int len)) return false;
            if (len < 0 || len > 32) return false;
            int valueConst = 0;
            if (isSet && !TryEvaluateConstant(args[1], out valueConst)) return false;
            // A zero-length expansion emits no address or fill evaluation in this helper.
            if (len == 0) return true;
            if (isSet)
            {
                int[] ptr = AcquireTemps(2);
                try
                {
                    EmitLoadValue(args[0], ctx, 2);
                    EmitAsm("STA", Mem(ptr[0]));
                    EmitAsm("STX", Mem(ptr[1]));
                    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++)
                    {
                        EmitAsm("LDY", Imm(i));
                        EmitAsm("LDA", Imm(valueConst));
                        EmitAsm("STA", IndY(ptr[0]));
                    }
                }
                finally { ReleaseTemps(ptr); }
                return true;
            }
            EmitFixedMemcpy(args[0], args[1], len, ctx);
            return true;
        }

void EmitFixedMemcpy(Expr dstExpr, Expr srcExpr, int len, FunctionContext ctx)
        {
            int[] ptr = AcquireTemps(4);
            try
            {
                EmitLoadValue(dstExpr, ctx, 2);
                EmitAsm("STA", Mem(ptr[0]));
                EmitAsm("STX", Mem(ptr[1]));
                EmitLoadValue(srcExpr, ctx, 2);
                EmitAsm("STA", Mem(ptr[2]));
                EmitAsm("STX", Mem(ptr[3]));
                for (int i = 0; i < len; i++)
                {
                    EmitAsm("LDY", Imm(i));
                    EmitAsm("LDA", IndY(ptr[2]));
                    EmitAsm("STA", IndY(ptr[0]));
                }
            }
            finally { ReleaseTemps(ptr); }
        }

__memset_small

Fill up to 255 consecutive bytes with one byte value, using an 8-bit count. This is suitable for initializing a small working buffer. Choose __memset when the required length exceeds 255 bytes.

Syntax

c
void __memset_small(u8* dst, u8 value, u8 len);

Parameters

dst

Pointer to the first writable destination byte. Reserve enough consecutive bytes for the complete operation; no buffer is allocated for you.

value

The byte repeated at every destination address: 0–255. Use 0 to clear the range. To initialize a u16 array to a nonzero numeric value, assign its elements individually instead.

len

Number of bytes as u8: 0–255. Do not pass 256 to mean a full 256-byte block; that length does not fit this parameter. Use the corresponding function without _small for 256 bytes or more.

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

A zero count transfers no bytes. Side effects in argument expressions still occur: the example calls two pointer-returning functions and observes both calls even though the copy length is zero.

The operation finishes before the caller continues. It neither switches ROM/RAM banks nor clips a range to a buffer boundary. Keep mappings stable, use valid memory ranges and coordinate access with interrupt handlers that use the same buffers.

On FC, dst is a CPU address, not a PPU address. Copying to CPU RAM does not update CHR, nametables or palettes; use PPU/VRAM APIs to upload that data. Generated helpers share argument/scratch storage, so do not re-enter them from NMI/IRQ while another call is in progress.

Usage example

c
memory_reset();
__memset_small(memory_destination+1,0x5A,255);
memory_fill_byte=memory_check(255,1);

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

This example uses __memset_small to fill 255 bytes at offset 1 with 0x5A. memory_check requires every byte in that range to equal 0x5A, while the guard bytes stay 0xCC and the separate source buffer remains untouched. The FILL BYTE row must show 255.

The complete program resets two 264-byte buffers before each operation, then checks every source byte, every destination byte and the untouched guard regions. The expected rows are COPY WORD 257, FILL WORD 257, COPY BYTE 255, FILL BYTE 255, COPY16 016, COPY32 032, ZERO CALLS 002 and FAILED 000. WORD/BYTE describe the count width, not the size of each copied item. The numbers are produced by the sample's checks, not return values from these void functions.

The captured screens show black lettering on white for DMG, blue on white for CGB and blue on black for FC. This example verifies RAM operations; the lettering presents the results rather than demonstrating a drawing primitive. Separate emulator checks cover 88 memory cases on each platform, including constant and runtime lengths at 0, 1, 16, 17, 32, 33, 64, 65 and 255 bytes, plus 256 and 257 for the word-count forms. bool TryEmitMemcpyOrMemsetInline(string funcName, Expr[] args, FunctionContext ctx, bool isSet, int lenIndex, int lenSize)
        {
            args = args ?? Array.Empty<Expr>();
            int expected = isSet ? 3 : 3;
            if (args.Length != expected) return false;
            if (!TryEvaluateConstant(args[lenIndex], out int len)) return false;
            if (len < 0 || len > 32) return false;
            int valueConst = 0;
            if (isSet && !TryEvaluateConstant(args[1], out valueConst)) return false;
            // A zero-length expansion emits no address or fill evaluation in this helper.
            if (len == 0) return true;
            if (isSet)
            {
                int[] ptr = AcquireTemps(2);
                try
                {
                    EmitLoadValue(args[0], ctx, 2);
                    EmitAsm("STA", Mem(ptr[0]));
                    EmitAsm("STX", Mem(ptr[1]));
                    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++)
                    {
                        EmitAsm("LDY", Imm(i));
                        EmitAsm("LDA", Imm(valueConst));
                        EmitAsm("STA", IndY(ptr[0]));
                    }
                }
                finally { ReleaseTemps(ptr); }
                return true;
            }
            EmitFixedMemcpy(args[0], args[1], len, ctx);
            return true;
        }

void EmitFixedMemcpy(Expr dstExpr, Expr srcExpr, int len, FunctionContext ctx)
        {
            int[] ptr = AcquireTemps(4);
            try
            {
                EmitLoadValue(dstExpr, ctx, 2);
                EmitAsm("STA", Mem(ptr[0]));
                EmitAsm("STX", Mem(ptr[1]));
                EmitLoadValue(srcExpr, ctx, 2);
                EmitAsm("STA", Mem(ptr[2]));
                EmitAsm("STX", Mem(ptr[3]));
                for (int i = 0; i < len; i++)
                {
                    EmitAsm("LDY", Imm(i));
                    EmitAsm("LDA", IndY(ptr[2]));
                    EmitAsm("STA", IndY(ptr[0]));
                }
            }
            finally { ReleaseTemps(ptr); }
        }

            if (newFunc.Match(Tag.Name, out string __sfname))

                    }
                    else

                        if (pty == null || !(pty.IsPointer || pty.IsArray))
                            Program.Error(expr.Source, ErrorCode.ExpectedType, "{0}: first argument must be a pointer or array, got: {1}", __sfname, (pty == null ? "<unknown>" : pty.Show()));

                    }

                    return Expr.Make(Tag.Slice, newArgs[0], newArgs[1]).WithSource(expr.Source);
                }
            }

            return MakeCall(newFunc, newArgs).WithSource(expr.Source);

__metasprite_draw

Expand a terminated stream of sprite parts into consecutive entries in the page-02 shadow buffer. Each part adds byte-sized X/Y offsets to the base position and supplies its own tile and attributes. Return the next OAM index.

Syntax

c
u8 __metasprite_draw(u8 oam_index, u8 base_x, u8 base_y, const u8* metasprite);

Parameters

oam_index

Sprite entry number, 0–63, not a byte offset. The implementation multiplies it by four using an 8-bit cursor; out-of-range values wrap modulo 64 and can overwrite another entry. No allocation check is performed.

base_x

Horizontal position in pixels, stored as an unsigned byte. This is a pixel coordinate, not a tile coordinate.

base_y

Raw OAM Y byte. Use visible_top-1 for a visible top below scanline zero; values 239..255 are outside the visible 240-line area.

metasprite

Pointer to readable four-byte records: dx, dy, tile, attr. A byte 0xFF in the next dx position ends the stream; no other bytes are needed after it. Offsets add modulo 256: 0xFE represents −2 and dy=0xFF can represent −1, but dx=0xFF is reserved and cannot represent −1. The pointer must remain valid in the currently mapped memory.

Return value

Next OAM entry number, (oam_index + parts_written) modulo 64. This is a cursor, not the number of parts drawn. For an empty stream it is oam_index modulo 64.

Conditions and limits

These operations edit CPU RAM at 0x0200–0x02FF; they do not immediately change hardware OAM. Transfer the completed page with __oam_dma. They do not maintain the sprite library’s allocation flags, coordinate arrays or active count. Keep interrupt handlers from editing or transferring a partially prepared page.

There is no part count, clipping or capacity check. Include a terminator and use at most 64−oam_index parts. Both coordinates wrap modulo 256; after slot 63 the write cursor wraps to slot 0. An empty stream changes no entries. This stream format differs from the counted MetaSpritePart array used by the sprite library’s metasprite_draw.

Usage example

c
fc_oam_next=__metasprite_draw(5,136,95,fc_oam_pair); // Returns 7 after two entries.

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

The example separates each operation into a labeled row. SET and MOVE show 8×8 right arrows at (144,16) and (144,32); TILE shows a green square at (144,48); ATTR shows the arrow flipped both ways at (144,64). HIDE at (144,80) and CLEAR at (144,112) must stay empty. META shows a pair at (136,96) and (144,96), with the second arrow mirrored horizontally. NEXT 07 is the next write position after writing slots 5 and 6. Arrows have red edges, green shafts and blue tip details. Verification compares 8,704 pixels per image and checks the transferred OAM bytes; physical hardware is untested.

TRANSFER shows an arrow at (144,128). This program sends page 02 directly with __oam_dma, including every field prepared by the individual sprite operations.

__mic_read2p

Read the digital signal for the second Famicom controller's microphone from $4016 bit 2. The helper reads the register once, masks 0x04 and normalizes the result to 0 or 1 without inversion. It does not latch controllers, record audio, measure volume or recognize speech.

Syntax

c
u8 __mic_read2p(void);

Return value

Exactly 1 when $4016 & 0x04 is nonzero, otherwise 0. This is the sampled digital level, not a button mask, amplitude, frequency or count of spoken words.

Conditions and limits

Although the microphone belongs to controller 2, this helper accesses $4016, not $4017. A register read can also advance the controller's serial stream while strobe is low, so do not insert microphone reads inside another controller's eight-bit read loop. No input-history cache is updated.

The published KUROSAKI controller model returns only D0 plus fixed bit 6. D1 and the microphone bit are therefore always 0 in that emulator, even while ordinary controller buttons are held. The supplied run verifies compilation, ordinary-button input and this zero-signal observation. Nonzero peripheral signals, electrical timing and real-device compatibility remain unverified; a zero here is not proof that an attached device works or that these functions cannot read it on hardware.

Usage example

c
mic_direct=__mic_read2p(); // A separate sample of the same digital signal.

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

This program contrasts ordinary D0 input with expansion D1 and the microphone's digital level. Hold A on controller 1 and B on controller 2 until the snapshot is captured. NORMAL P1 and NORMAL P2 display 001 and 002. In the supplied KUROSAKI run, D1 PORT 1, D1 PORT 2, EXP ALIAS 1, EXP ALIAS 2, MIC LEVEL and MIC DIRECT all display 000 because those signal lines are not emulated. The displayed values then stay fixed. With suitable peripherals and an implementation of their signal lines, the expansion and microphone values depend on the actual inputs; consult the bit layouts above rather than expecting these zeros.

__midi_clock

Send one timing-clock byte F8. The caller schedules repeated ticks.

Syntax

c
void __midi_clock(void);

Return value

No return value. Changes sound registers or driver state.

Conditions and limits

Requires an external circuit connecting $4016 D0 to TX and $4017 D4 to RX. A standard controller does not provide MIDI and these calls do not play the internal APU. Stop DMC playback/DMA and mask NMI and IRQ during transfers; avoid concurrent port/shared-scratch access. NTSC’s 57 cycles/bit give about 31,400 bps, roughly +0.5% from 31,250. PAL timing and round-trip communication with a physical adapter are unverified.

Usage example

c
// Controller-port byte encoding. This does not synthesize sound inside the FC.
#define SOUND_PORT_ONLY
#include "fc_sound_example.h"
void main(void) {
    sound_begin("MIDI PORT BYTES");
    // sound_begin has disabled DMC DMA and all internal APU voices. A compatible external circuit is required.
    // Stop NMI and mask IRQ so neither can split a software-timed serial frame.
    __ppu_ctrl_set(0); __irq_disable();
    __midi_out_byte(0x7E);
    __midi_program_change(2,5);
    __midi_control_change(2,7,100);
    __midi_note_on(2,69,96);
    __midi_note_off(2,69,0);
    __midi_clock(); __midi_start(); __midi_continue(); __midi_stop();
    // The emulator's unconnected input bit is low. Reading returns zero here.
    // A real input held high would block waiting for its start bit, without timeout.
    sound_result[0]=__midi_in_byte();
    sound_result[1]=1;
    __ppu_ctrl_set(0x80); __irq_enable();
    sound_end();
}

Expected result

The screen says EXTERNAL PORT DATA and no internal voice sounds. Transmitted bytes in hexadecimal are 7E; C2 05; B2 07 64; 92 45 60; 82 45 00; F8 FA FB FC. The check requires 57-cycle NTSC transmit cells and 57-cycle data-read spacing. Received 00 comes from the emulator’s unconnected input and does not prove communication with an external device.

__midi_continue

Send one realtime Continue byte FB without operating the internal music driver.

Syntax

c
void __midi_continue(void);

Return value

No return value. Changes sound registers or driver state.

Conditions and limits

Requires an external circuit connecting $4016 D0 to TX and $4017 D4 to RX. A standard controller does not provide MIDI and these calls do not play the internal APU. Stop DMC playback/DMA and mask NMI and IRQ during transfers; avoid concurrent port/shared-scratch access. NTSC’s 57 cycles/bit give about 31,400 bps, roughly +0.5% from 31,250. PAL timing and round-trip communication with a physical adapter are unverified.

Usage example

c
// Controller-port byte encoding. This does not synthesize sound inside the FC.
#define SOUND_PORT_ONLY
#include "fc_sound_example.h"
void main(void) {
    sound_begin("MIDI PORT BYTES");
    // sound_begin has disabled DMC DMA and all internal APU voices. A compatible external circuit is required.
    // Stop NMI and mask IRQ so neither can split a software-timed serial frame.
    __ppu_ctrl_set(0); __irq_disable();
    __midi_out_byte(0x7E);
    __midi_program_change(2,5);
    __midi_control_change(2,7,100);
    __midi_note_on(2,69,96);
    __midi_note_off(2,69,0);
    __midi_clock(); __midi_start(); __midi_continue(); __midi_stop();
    // The emulator's unconnected input bit is low. Reading returns zero here.
    // A real input held high would block waiting for its start bit, without timeout.
    sound_result[0]=__midi_in_byte();
    sound_result[1]=1;
    __ppu_ctrl_set(0x80); __irq_enable();
    sound_end();
}

Expected result

The screen says EXTERNAL PORT DATA and no internal voice sounds. Transmitted bytes in hexadecimal are 7E; C2 05; B2 07 64; 92 45 60; 82 45 00; F8 FA FB FC. The check requires 57-cycle NTSC transmit cells and 57-cycle data-read spacing. Received 00 comes from the emulator’s unconnected input and does not prove communication with an external device.

__midi_note_on

Send note-on as three bytes: 0x90 | (ch & 0x0F), note, velocity.

Syntax

c
void __midi_note_on(u8 ch, u8 note, u8 velocity);

Parameters

ch

MIDI channel 0..15; the low nibble enters the status byte. Zero corresponds to displayed MIDI channel 1.

note

MIDI note 0..127; 69 is A4. The helper does not mask to seven bits, so the caller enforces the range.

velocity

Velocity 0..127; not automatically masked to seven bits.

Return value

No return value. Changes sound registers or driver state.

Conditions and limits

Requires an external circuit connecting $4016 D0 to TX and $4017 D4 to RX. A standard controller does not provide MIDI and these calls do not play the internal APU. Stop DMC playback/DMA and mask NMI and IRQ during transfers; avoid concurrent port/shared-scratch access. NTSC’s 57 cycles/bit give about 31,400 bps, roughly +0.5% from 31,250. PAL timing and round-trip communication with a physical adapter are unverified.

Usage example

c
// Controller-port byte encoding. This does not synthesize sound inside the FC.
#define SOUND_PORT_ONLY
#include "fc_sound_example.h"
void main(void) {
    sound_begin("MIDI PORT BYTES");
    // sound_begin has disabled DMC DMA and all internal APU voices. A compatible external circuit is required.
    // Stop NMI and mask IRQ so neither can split a software-timed serial frame.
    __ppu_ctrl_set(0); __irq_disable();
    __midi_out_byte(0x7E);
    __midi_program_change(2,5);
    __midi_control_change(2,7,100);
    __midi_note_on(2,69,96);
    __midi_note_off(2,69,0);
    __midi_clock(); __midi_start(); __midi_continue(); __midi_stop();
    // The emulator's unconnected input bit is low. Reading returns zero here.
    // A real input held high would block waiting for its start bit, without timeout.
    sound_result[0]=__midi_in_byte();
    sound_result[1]=1;
    __ppu_ctrl_set(0x80); __irq_enable();
    sound_end();
}

Expected result

The screen says EXTERNAL PORT DATA and no internal voice sounds. Transmitted bytes in hexadecimal are 7E; C2 05; B2 07 64; 92 45 60; 82 45 00; F8 FA FB FC. The check requires 57-cycle NTSC transmit cells and 57-cycle data-read spacing. Received 00 comes from the emulator’s unconnected input and does not prove communication with an external device.

Complete example program

Build command

powershell

.\kitaqfc\kitaqfc.exe .\kitaq-docs\samples\api-examples\fc\sound_midi.c -I .\kitaqfc\lib -I .\kitaq-docs\samples -o .\out\fc-midi.nes --mapper=nrom --nes-chr=.\kitaq-docs\samples\font.chr --no-cache --no-disasm

EmitHelperStart("__kq_midi_out_a");
            bool midiScratchInZeroPage = _runtimeIntrinsicTmp0Address <= 0xFF;
            EmitAsm("STA", Mem(_runtimeIntrinsicTmp0Address));
            EmitAsm("LDA", Imm(0));
            EmitAsm("STA", Mem(0x4016));
            // Unroll so neither branch cost nor payload bits change the baud.
            // Each data edge: 44 NOP cycles + LSR zp (5) + LDA/ADC (4) + STA (4).
            for (int bit = 0; bit < 8; bit++)
            {
                for (int delay = 0; delay < (midiScratchInZeroPage ? 22 : 20); delay++) EmitAsm("NOP");
                if (!midiScratchInZeroPage) EmitAsm("BIT", Mem(CallArgBase));
                EmitAsm("LSR", Mem(_runtimeIntrinsicTmp0Address));
                EmitAsm("LDA", Imm(0));
                EmitAsm("ADC", Imm(0));
                EmitAsm("STA", Mem(0x4016));
            }
            // 51 delay cycles plus LDA/STA (6) place the stop bit 57 cycles later.
            for (int delay = 0; delay < 24; delay++) EmitAsm("NOP");
            EmitAsm("BIT", Mem(CallArgBase));
            EmitAsm("LDA", Imm(1));
            EmitAsm("STA", Mem(0x4016));
            EmitMidiBitDelay(); // Hold stop high for at least one full bit cell.
            EmitAsm("RTS");

            EmitHelperStart("__midi_out_byte");
            EmitAsm("LDA", Mem(CallArgBase));
            EmitAsm("JSR", Abs("__kq_midi_out_a"));
            EmitAsm("RTS");

            // Poll in nine-cycle steps, then sample near data-bit centers.
            // IRQ/NMI masking belongs to the caller; no timeout/framing status is returned.
            EmitHelperStart("__midi_in_byte");
            EmitAsm("LDA", Imm(0));
            EmitAsm("STA", Mem(_runtimeIntrinsicTmp0Address));
            string waitStart = NewGeneratedLabel("midi_wait_start");
            _assembly.Add(Expr.Make(Tag.Label, waitStart));
            EmitAsm("LDA", Mem(0x4017));
            EmitAsm("AND", Imm(0x10));
            EmitAsm("BNE", Rel(waitStart));
            // 81 cycles from the start-detect read to the first data read.
            // Polling uncertainty is at most nine cycles within a 57-cycle cell.
            for (int delay = 0; delay < 35; delay++) EmitAsm("NOP");
            EmitAsm("BIT", Mem(CallArgBase));
            for (int bit = 0; bit < 8; bit++)
            {
                EmitAsm("LDA", Mem(0x4017));
                EmitAsm("AND", Imm(0x10));
                EmitAsm("CMP", Imm(0x10));
                EmitAsm("ROR", Mem(_runtimeIntrinsicTmp0Address));
                for (int delay = 0; delay < (midiScratchInZeroPage ? 22 : 20); delay++) EmitAsm("NOP");
                if (!midiScratchInZeroPage) EmitAsm("BIT", Mem(CallArgBase));
            }
            EmitAsm("LDA", Mem(_runtimeIntrinsicTmp0Address));
            EmitAsm("RTS");

__midi_stop

Send one realtime Stop byte FC. This does not directly silence the APU or previously sent notes.

Syntax

c
void __midi_stop(void);

Return value

No return value. Changes sound registers or driver state.

Conditions and limits

Requires an external circuit connecting $4016 D0 to TX and $4017 D4 to RX. A standard controller does not provide MIDI and these calls do not play the internal APU. Stop DMC playback/DMA and mask NMI and IRQ during transfers; avoid concurrent port/shared-scratch access. NTSC’s 57 cycles/bit give about 31,400 bps, roughly +0.5% from 31,250. PAL timing and round-trip communication with a physical adapter are unverified.

Usage example

c
// Controller-port byte encoding. This does not synthesize sound inside the FC.
#define SOUND_PORT_ONLY
#include "fc_sound_example.h"
void main(void) {
    sound_begin("MIDI PORT BYTES");
    // sound_begin has disabled DMC DMA and all internal APU voices. A compatible external circuit is required.
    // Stop NMI and mask IRQ so neither can split a software-timed serial frame.
    __ppu_ctrl_set(0); __irq_disable();
    __midi_out_byte(0x7E);
    __midi_program_change(2,5);
    __midi_control_change(2,7,100);
    __midi_note_on(2,69,96);
    __midi_note_off(2,69,0);
    __midi_clock(); __midi_start(); __midi_continue(); __midi_stop();
    // The emulator's unconnected input bit is low. Reading returns zero here.
    // A real input held high would block waiting for its start bit, without timeout.
    sound_result[0]=__midi_in_byte();
    sound_result[1]=1;
    __ppu_ctrl_set(0x80); __irq_enable();
    sound_end();
}

Expected result

The screen says EXTERNAL PORT DATA and no internal voice sounds. Transmitted bytes in hexadecimal are 7E; C2 05; B2 07 64; 92 45 60; 82 45 00; F8 FA FB FC. The check requires 57-cycle NTSC transmit cells and 57-cycle data-read spacing. Received 00 comes from the emulator’s unconnected input and does not prove communication with an external device.

Complete example program

Build command

powershell
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force .\out | Out-Null
.\kitaqfc\kitaqfc.exe .\kitaq-docs\samples\api-examples\fc\sound_midi.c -I .\kitaqfc\lib -I .\kitaq-docs\samples -o .\out\fc-midi.nes --mapper=nrom --nes-chr=.\kitaq-docs\samples\font.chr --no-cache --no-disasm

__mirroring_set

Map the four logical nametable regions onto the console’s two pages of screen RAM, for scrolling layouts or single-screen page selection.

Syntax

c
void __mirroring_set(u8 mode);

Parameters

mode

Mode numbers vary by board. MMC1/SUROM: 0=lower single screen, 1=upper single screen, 2=vertical, 3=horizontal. MMC3: 0=vertical, 1=horizontal. MMC5: 0=horizontal, 1=vertical, 2=lower single screen, 3=upper single screen. AxROM: 0=lower single screen, 1=upper single screen. FME7: 0=vertical, 1=horizontal, 2=lower single screen, 3=upper single screen. MMC3/AxROM use the low bit; the others use the low two bits.

Return value

No return value.

Conditions and limits

Intrinsic declarations are in intrinsics.h. Include nes_game.h for the nes_mapper_irq_* macros. Select the board at build time with --mapper.

Vertical mirroring aliases the four regions as A B A B; horizontal mirroring gives A A B B. Lower single screen gives A A A A and upper single screen B B B B. This changes memory mapping; it neither flips nor copies background graphics. Unsupported boards, including fixed-mirroring NROM, are rejected at build time.

MMC1 writes control $0C|mode, selecting a fixed upper 16 KiB PRG window and 8 KiB CHR mode. SUROM also updates its control shadow. AxROM changes the screen bit while retaining the runtime PRG bank value. If you also write mapper registers directly, keep them consistent with the runtime bank state.

For MMC5 the API writes $50/$44/$00/$55 to $5105. These arrangements use only the console’s two CIRAM pages. ExRAM and fill mode are outside this API. KUROSAKI supports all sixteen CIRAM-only arrangements; MMC5 ExRAM and fill rendering remain unsupported.

Change the sample’s --mapper=mmc3 to mmc1, mmc5, axrom or fme7 to inspect each board. The sample initializes MMC5/FME7 font CHR banks through their board registers.

Usage example

c
k=1;
    for (i=0;i<4;i++) {
        __mirroring_set(i);
        for (j=0;j<4;j++) { mirror_result[k]=mirror_read(0x2000+(u16)j*1024); k++; }
    }

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

The lesson writes 17 to the lower physical RAM page and 34 to the upper page, then reads the four logical regions. A denotes the lower page and B the upper page. Regions with the same letter share RAM, so a write through one is visible through the others. Columns are $2000, $2400, $2800 and $2C00; rows are modes 0..3. Text is displayed after the readback.

Complete example program

Build command

powershell
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force .\out | Out-Null
.\kitaqfc\kitaqfc.exe .\kitaq-docs\samples\api-examples\fc\mapper_mirroring.c -I .\kitaqfc\lib -I .\kitaq-docs\samples -o .\out\mapper_mirroring.nes --mapper=mmc3 --nes-chr=.\kitaq-docs\samples\font.chr --no-cache --no-disasm

__mul16x8

Compute a unsigned multiplication.

Syntax

c
u16 __mul16x8(u16 a, u8 b);

Parameters

a

Unsigned word, 0..65535.

b

Unsigned coefficient, 0..255.

Return value

Returns the low 16 bits of a*b.

Conditions and limits

On FC, q8_8/q1_7 names still use raw integer products without a fixed-point downshift. The Q1.7 functions alias their corresponding signed operations. The caller handles units; signed results are returned as u16 bit patterns.

Usage example

c
// Compare literal coefficients with values read from RAM.
result[2]=__mul16x8(513,127);
v0=513;v1=127;
result[3]=__mul16x8(v0,v1);

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

Compare literal inputs with values stored in RAM. Representative results appear as unsigned 16-bit values; negatives use two’s-complement bit patterns. GB rescales fixed-point products, while FC returns integer products, so identical inputs need not give identical results.

The excerpt stores these 16-bit values: result[2]=65151, result[3]=65151. Each literal-input calculation matches its RAM-input counterpart. The screen shows representative values; the result array holds every result.

Complete example program

__nametable_put

Write one tile byte directly to nametable 0 at PPU address 0x2000 + y*32 + x. The helper resets the latch before setting the address. It does not write tile graphics or palette attributes and does not clip coordinates.

Syntax

c
void __nametable_put(u8 x, u8 y, u8 tile);

Parameters

x / y

Tile coordinates, not pixels. Keep x in 0..31 and y in 0..29 for the visible 32×30 tile map. Each tile covers 8×8 pixels. The byte arguments are not clamped; invalid coordinates can write outside the intended tile area.

tile

Tile number 0..255 in the background pattern table selected by PPUCTRL. It selects existing CHR graphics; it is not a pixel color or a source-data pointer.

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

Direct PPU access requires rendering to be off or the entire operation to fit a safe VBlank interval. These functions do not wait, queue, mask NMI or restore scroll. Prevent an interrupt from changing the shared latch/address during the call. PPUCTRL bit 2 selects a destination step of 1 or 32 per data byte. The PPU handles mirroring and address wrapping; CHR-ROM cannot be written. Set the intended scroll state after access and before rendering.

NESdev: PPU registers

NESdev: PPU scrolling

Usage example

c
__nametable_put(2,12,1); // Blue solid marker at (16,96).

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

This program teaches register setup, direct tile/attribute writes, scrolling and separate background/sprite palette loads. The blue band at (0,16) measures 256×16 pixels: its first row repeats a solid 8×8 tile, a left-half 4×8 bar and an eight-row triangle; its second row contains only left-half bars. A solid green 64×32 rectangle starts at (16,48). A red 64×32 region at (144,48) contains an 8-by-4 grid of triangle tiles.

At y=96, blue markers at x=16, 24 and 32 are respectively a square, left-half bar and triangle; a red left-half bar is at x=80 and a green triangle at x=144. These are background tiles. At y=144, the separately colored sprites are a red 8×8 square at x=16, a blue left-half 4×8 bar at x=80 and a green eight-row triangle at x=144. Final scrolling is (0,0).

The image checks 16,384 pixels for the expected shapes and colors, including sprite colors. Separate state tests cover 31 cases: register replacement, status/latch effects, saved scroll coordinates, zero/255-byte transfers, increments 1/32, map edges, zero rectangle dimensions, table selectors, whole-byte attributes and both palette targets. Values of Y=255 are checked as register writes, not as correct scrolling artwork. Evidence is from KUROSAKI with NROM; real hardware is not tested.

void __nametable_rect(u8 x, u8 y, u8 w, u8 h, u8 tile);

x / y

Tile coordinates, not pixels. Keep x in 0..31 and y in 0..29 for the visible 32×30 tile map. Each tile covers 8×8 pixels. The byte arguments are not clamped; invalid coordinates can write outside the intended tile area.

w / h

Width and height in tiles, each an unsigned byte. Keep x+w<=32 and y+h<=30. Height zero performs no PPU accesses. Width zero writes no tile bytes, but still resets the latch and seeks each of the h row addresses. Use PPU increment 1 for horizontal rows.

__nmi_disable

Disable NMI generation at the PPU by clearing bit 7 of the compiler's PPUCTRL shadow and writing it to $2000. Preserve its other bits. This neither changes the CPU IRQ mask nor turns off rendering.

Syntax

c
void __nmi_disable(void);

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

These setters use the PPUCTRL shadow, not hardware readback; direct writes to $2000 do not update that shadow. Enabling NMI while the VBlank flag is set can trigger it immediately. Disabling PPU generation cannot cancel a request already latched by the CPU.

NESdev: NMI

NESdev: CPU interrupts

Usage example

c
__nmi_disable();
before_count=__nmi_ready();
for(i=0;i<2000;i++)frozen=__nmi_ready();
frozen=(u8)(frozen-before_count); // No default-handler advances while off.

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

The program shows how the CPU IRQ mask differs from PPU NMI control. On the black screen, blue text must show IRQ DISABLED I = 001, IRQ ENABLED I = 000, SAVED SECTION I = 001 and RESTORED I = 000. Each value is the extracted I bit, not the whole status byte. FAILED CHECKS must be 000.

Run for at least 360 emulator frames so the 256-wait demonstration can finish. NMI DELTA 3 WAITS must be 003 even with IRQ masked; NMI DELTA 256 WAITS must be 000 because the byte wraps. NMI OFF DELTA must be 000. This program uses the default handler without runtime.c. Separate state checks cover 21 cases, including status-bit restoration and bounded waits with NMI disabled or an empty custom handler. KUROSAKI/NROM is tested; physical hardware is not.

Enable PPU-generated NMI by setting bit 7 of the compiler's PPUCTRL shadow, then writing that byte to $2000. The other shadow bits and the CPU IRQ mask are preserved. This does not enable background or sprite rendering.

Syntax

Expected result

The program shows how the CPU IRQ mask differs from PPU NMI control. On the black screen, blue text must show IRQ DISABLED I = 001, IRQ ENABLED I = 000, SAVED SECTION I = 001 and RESTORED I = 000. Each value is the extracted I bit, not the whole status byte. FAILED CHECKS must be 000.

Run for at least 360 emulator frames so the 256-wait demonstration can finish. NMI DELTA 3 WAITS must be 003 even with IRQ masked; NMI DELTA 256 WAITS must be 000 because the byte wraps. NMI OFF DELTA must be 000. This program uses the default handler without runtime.c. Separate state checks cover 21 cases, including status-bit restoration and bounded waits with NMI disabled or an empty custom handler. KUROSAKI/NROM is tested; physical hardware is not.

__nmi_ready

Read the compiler's current NMI counter without waiting or clearing it. Despite the name, the result is a counter byte rather than a Boolean ready flag. Compare it with a saved value to detect progress by the default NMI handler.

Syntax

c
u8 __nmi_ready(void);

Return value

An unsigned byte, 0–255, incremented modulo 256 by the default NMI handler. Zero is valid. After 256 advances the saved and current values match again; infrequent polling cannot count arbitrarily long intervals.

Conditions and limits

This counter belongs to the compiler's default NMI handler. Defining __nes_nmi replaces that handler. runtime.c uses its own nes_nmi_counter and nes_wait_nmi. An empty custom handler leaves the compiler counter unchanged, so __nmi_wait never returns. Enable NMI and call the wait outside the NMI handler.

__nmi_wait

Read the compiler's NMI counter on entry and busy-wait until its value changes. With the default NMI handler, this waits for a subsequent handler completion, including execution of committed VRAM-queue work. The call does not enable NMI, commit queued commands or impose a timeout.

An empty custom handler leaves the compiler counter unchanged, so __nmi_wait never returns. Enable NMI and call the wait outside the NMI handler.

__oam_clear

Hide all 64 sprites in the page-02 shadow buffer by setting each Y byte to 0xF0. Tile numbers, attributes and X coordinates remain unchanged.

Syntax

c
void __oam_clear(void);

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

These operations edit CPU RAM at 0x0200–0x02FF; they do not immediately change hardware OAM. Transfer the completed page with __oam_dma. They do not maintain the sprite library’s allocation flags, coordinate arrays or active count. Keep interrupt handlers from editing or transferring a partially prepared page.

Usage example

c
__sprite_set(63,144,111,128,0); // Seed the CLEAR row with a visible entry.
__oam_clear(); // Set every Y byte to 240; tile, attributes and X are retained.

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

The example separates each operation into a labeled row. SET and MOVE show 8×8 right arrows at (144,16) and (144,32); TILE shows a green square at (144,48); ATTR shows the arrow flipped both ways at (144,64). HIDE at (144,80) and CLEAR at (144,112) must stay empty. META shows a pair at (136,96) and (144,96), with the second arrow mirrored horizontally. NEXT 07 is the next write position after writing slots 5 and 6. Arrows have red edges, green shafts and blue tip details. Verification compares 8,704 pixels per image and checks the transferred OAM bytes; physical hardware is untested.

TRANSFER shows an arrow at (144,128). This program sends page 02 directly with __oam_dma, including every field prepared by the individual sprite operations.

__oam_dma

Transfer the complete 256-byte shadow page at 0x0200–0x02FF to hardware OAM, starting at OAM entry 0. The CPU pauses during the transfer and resumes after it finishes.

Syntax

c
void __oam_dma(void);

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

Call during VBlank or with rendering disabled; neither DMA intrinsic waits for VBlank. Both set OAMADDR to zero before transfer. Hardware DMA normally stalls the CPU for 513 or 514 cycles; DMC activity can extend it. KUROSAKI approximates this as 513 cycles, so its image verification does not establish exact hardware timing. KQ2421 can still be emitted after an explicit VBlank wait because the compiler classifies the caller by name.

Usage example

c
m_wait();__oam_dma(); // Transfer all 256 bytes from page 02 at VBlank.

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

The example separates each operation into a labeled row. SET and MOVE show 8×8 right arrows at (144,16) and (144,32); TILE shows a green square at (144,48); ATTR shows the arrow flipped both ways at (144,64). HIDE at (144,80) and CLEAR at (144,112) must stay empty. META shows a pair at (136,96) and (144,96), with the second arrow mirrored horizontally. NEXT 07 is the next write position after writing slots 5 and 6. Arrows have red edges, green shafts and blue tip details. Verification compares 8,704 pixels per image and checks the transferred OAM bytes; physical hardware is untested.

TRANSFER shows an arrow at (144,128). This program sends page 02 directly with __oam_dma, including every field prepared by the individual sprite operations.

__oam_dma_page

Transfer 256 bytes from the selected CPU memory page to hardware OAM, starting at entry 0. This permits a separate prepared OAM page without copying it into page 02 first. The selected source is not modified.

Syntax

c
void __oam_dma_page(u8 page);

Parameters

page

High byte of the source CPU address: pass 4 for 0x0400–0x04FF, not 0x0400. Supply a complete readable 256-byte page and keep any required bank mapped. Avoid pages containing I/O registers, whose reads can have side effects. No source validation is performed.

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

Call during VBlank or with rendering disabled; neither DMA intrinsic waits for VBlank. Both set OAMADDR to zero before transfer. Hardware DMA normally stalls the CPU for 513 or 514 cycles; DMC activity can extend it. KUROSAKI approximates this as 513 cycles, so its image verification does not establish exact hardware timing. KQ2421 can still be emitted after an explicit VBlank wait because the compiler classifies the caller by name.

This variant copies the prepared page 02 into a separate array at 0x0400, then changes only entry 7’s tile to 129. __oam_dma_page(4) must show a green square at (144,128) beside TRANSFER, while page 02 still contains the arrow’s tile 128. All other rows match the default-page example. The check compares all 256 hardware OAM bytes with page 04 and confirms that page 02 was not changed.

__pad_buttons

Keep bits 0–3 of the supplied NES pad snapshot (pad & 0x0F): A, B, Select and Start. This only filters a value already read; it does not access controller hardware.

Syntax

c
u8 __pad_buttons(u8 pad);

Parameters

pad

An already sampled 8-bit NES pad value, such as the result of __pad_read1_safe(). Supply the value itself, not a pointer, a port number or an input_* logical mask.

Return value

A mask from 0 to 15 in the bit order described above. More than one bit can be set; test a button with result & bit, rather than comparing the whole result to 1.

Conditions and limits

NES raw layout: A=0x01, B=0x02, SELECT=0x04, START=0x08, UP=0x10, DOWN=0x20, LEFT=0x40, RIGHT=0x80. A set bit means pressed. Use these values with nes_pad_* and raw __pad_* results, not the shared BTN_* masks from input.h.

Usage example

c
buttons=__pad_buttons(raw1); // Low nibble of 129: 1, the A button.

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

This program compares both controller ports, ordinary and repeated reads, mask filters and the shorthand macros. Hold A + Right on controller 1 and B + Left on controller 2. RAW P1, SAFE P1 and ALIAS P1 are 129; the three P2 values are 66. BUTTONS P1 is 1 and DIRS P1 is 128: filtering directions preserves their high-bit positions. FAILED CHECKS must be 0. The captured values remain on screen.

__pad_read1

Latch both controllers with a 1-to-0 write to $4016, then read the eight D0 serial bits from controller 1 at $4016. Return one NES-format held-button snapshot without retrying or calculating edges.

Syntax

c
u8 __pad_read1(void);

Return value

An 8-bit held-button mask in NES raw order. Each set bit identifies a pressed button; 0 means none. It is not a normalized Boolean.

Conditions and limits

NES raw layout: A=0x01, B=0x02, SELECT=0x04, START=0x08, UP=0x10, DOWN=0x20, LEFT=0x40, RIGHT=0x80. A set bit means pressed. Use these values with nes_pad_* and raw __pad_* results, not the shared BTN_* masks from input.h.

This call reads a fresh hardware snapshot; it does not update input_* or nes_pad1_* cached state and does not generate pressed/released edges or repeats. Read once, save the result, and derive edges against your saved previous mask when needed.

Usage example

__pad_read1_d1

Read eight serial bits from expansion input D1 at $4016. Write 1 then 0 to $4016 to latch the controller streams, sample bit 1 eight times, and place successive samples into result bits 0–7. This is one read of the D1 channel for port 1; it does not read the ordinary D0 controller channel or retry for matching samples.

Syntax

c
u8 __pad_read1_d1(void);

Return value

An 8-bit held-button mask in NES raw order. Each set bit identifies a pressed button; 0 means none. It is not a normalized Boolean.

Conditions and limits

NES raw layout: A=0x01, B=0x02, SELECT=0x04, START=0x08, UP=0x10, DOWN=0x20, LEFT=0x40, RIGHT=0x80. A set bit means pressed. Use these values with nes_pad_* and raw __pad_* results, not the shared BTN_* masks from input.h.

Use a peripheral that supplies a compatible eight-bit serial pad stream on the selected D1 line. The function does not detect the attached device or implement every expansion-device protocol. Each call strobes both controller streams; finish a complete read before starting another. Results are fresh snapshots and do not update the input_* or nes_pad1_* caches.

The published KUROSAKI controller model returns only D0 plus fixed bit 6. D1 and the microphone bit are therefore always 0 in that emulator, even while ordinary controller buttons are held. The supplied run verifies compilation, ordinary-button input and this zero-signal observation. Nonzero peripheral signals, electrical timing and real-device compatibility remain unverified; a zero here is not proof that an attached device works or that these functions cannot read it on hardware.

Usage example

c
d1_first=__pad_read1_d1();

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

This program contrasts ordinary D0 input with expansion D1 and the microphone's digital level. Hold A on controller 1 and B on controller 2 until the snapshot is captured. NORMAL P1 and NORMAL P2 display 001 and 002. In the supplied KUROSAKI run, D1 PORT 1, D1 PORT 2, EXP ALIAS 1, EXP ALIAS 2, MIC LEVEL and MIC DIRECT all display 000 because those signal lines are not emulated. The displayed values then stay fixed. With suitable peripherals and an implementation of their signal lines, the expansion and microphone values depend on the actual inputs; consult the bit layouts above rather than expecting these zeros.

The published KUROSAKI controller model returns only D0 plus fixed bit 6. D1 and the microphone bit are therefore always 0 in that emulator, even while ordinary controller buttons are held. The supplied run verifies compilation, ordinary-button input and this zero-signal observation. Nonzero peripheral signals, electrical timing and real-device compatibility remain unverified; a zero here is not proof that an attached device works or that these functions cannot read it on hardware.

__pad_read1_safe

Sample controller 1 using repeated pairs of complete __pad_read1() calls. Return the NES-format mask when both reads in a pair agree. This returns a held snapshot, not new-press events.

Syntax

c
u8 __pad_read1_safe(void);

Return value

An 8-bit held-button mask in NES raw order. Each set bit identifies a pressed button; 0 means none. It is not a normalized Boolean.

Conditions and limits

NES raw layout: A=0x01, B=0x02, SELECT=0x04, START=0x08, UP=0x10, DOWN=0x20, LEFT=0x40, RIGHT=0x80. A set bit means pressed. Use these values with nes_pad_* and raw __pad_* results, not the shared BTN_* masks from input.h.

This call reads a fresh hardware snapshot; it does not update input_* or nes_pad1_* cached state and does not generate pressed/released edges or repeats. Read once, save the result, and derive edges against your saved previous mask when needed.

The safe reader performs pairs of complete reads until the two masks match. Each read strobes $4016, restarting both controllers' serial streams. There is no retry limit. This consistency check does not establish compatibility with every DMC/peripheral combination.

Usage example

c
safe1=__pad_read1_safe(); // Repeat paired controller-1 reads until they agree.

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

This program compares both controller ports, ordinary and repeated reads, mask filters and the shorthand macros. Hold A + Right on controller 1 and B + Left on controller 2. RAW P1, SAFE P1 and ALIAS P1 are 129; the three P2 values are 66. BUTTONS P1 is 1 and DIRS P1 is 128: filtering directions preserves their high-bit positions. FAILED CHECKS must be 0. The captured values remain on screen.

__pad_read2_d1

Read eight serial bits from expansion input D1 at $4017. Write 1 then 0 to $4016 to latch the controller streams, sample bit 1 eight times, and place successive samples into result bits 0–7. This is one read of the D1 channel for port 2; it does not read the ordinary D0 controller channel or retry for matching samples.

Syntax

c
u8 __pad_read2_d1(void);

Return value

An 8-bit held-button mask in NES raw order. Each set bit identifies a pressed button; 0 means none. It is not a normalized Boolean.

Conditions and limits

NES raw layout: A=0x01, B=0x02, SELECT=0x04, START=0x08, UP=0x10, DOWN=0x20, LEFT=0x40, RIGHT=0x80. A set bit means pressed. Use these values with nes_pad_* and raw __pad_* results, not the shared BTN_* masks from input.h.

Use a peripheral that supplies a compatible eight-bit serial pad stream on the selected D1 line. The function does not detect the attached device or implement every expansion-device protocol. Each call strobes both controller streams; finish a complete read before starting another. Results are fresh snapshots and do not update the input_* or nes_pad1_* caches.

The published KUROSAKI controller model returns only D0 plus fixed bit 6. D1 and the microphone bit are therefore always 0 in that emulator, even while ordinary controller buttons are held. The supplied run verifies compilation, ordinary-button input and this zero-signal observation. Nonzero peripheral signals, electrical timing and real-device compatibility remain unverified; a zero here is not proof that an attached device works or that these functions cannot read it on hardware.

Usage example

c
d1_second=__pad_read2_d1();

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

This program contrasts ordinary D0 input with expansion D1 and the microphone's digital level. Hold A on controller 1 and B on controller 2 until the snapshot is captured. NORMAL P1 and NORMAL P2 display 001 and 002. In the supplied KUROSAKI run, D1 PORT 1, D1 PORT 2, EXP ALIAS 1, EXP ALIAS 2, MIC LEVEL and MIC DIRECT all display 000 because those signal lines are not emulated. The displayed values then stay fixed. With suitable peripherals and an implementation of their signal lines, the expansion and microphone values depend on the actual inputs; consult the bit layouts above rather than expecting these zeros.

__palette_bg_load

Reset the PPU latch, set address 0x3F00 and write exactly 16 source bytes through PPUDATA for the four background palettes. This is an immediate transfer; it does not change nametable attribute selections or load tile graphics.

Syntax

c
void __palette_bg_load(const u8* pal16);

Parameters

pal16

CPU pointer to 16 readable NES palette-code bytes. These are palette codes, not RGB triplets. Keep the source bank mapped until the synchronous call returns; no bank switching or length check is performed. Use PPU increment 1 to reach the intended 16 palette addresses.

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

PPU addresses 0x3F10/14/18/1C alias 0x3F00/04/08/0C. Loading the sprite palette therefore also writes those background entries. The compiler sends the supplied bytes unchanged; it does not validate color choices, merge palettes or preserve the aliased entries.

Direct PPU access requires rendering to be off or the entire operation to fit a safe VBlank interval. These functions do not wait, queue, mask NMI or restore scroll. Prevent an interrupt from changing the shared latch/address during the call. PPUCTRL bit 2 selects a destination step of 1 or 32 per data byte. The PPU handles mirroring and address wrapping; CHR-ROM cannot be written. Set the intended scroll state after access and before rendering.

NESdev: PPU registers

NESdev: PPU scrolling

Usage example

c
__palette_bg_load(scene_palette); // Four background palettes, 16 bytes total.

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

This program teaches register setup, direct tile/attribute writes, scrolling and separate background/sprite palette loads. The blue band at (0,16) measures 256×16 pixels: its first row repeats a solid 8×8 tile, a left-half 4×8 bar and an eight-row triangle; its second row contains only left-half bars. A solid green 64×32 rectangle starts at (16,48). A red 64×32 region at (144,48) contains an 8-by-4 grid of triangle tiles.

At y=96, blue markers at x=16, 24 and 32 are respectively a square, left-half bar and triangle; a red left-half bar is at x=80 and a green triangle at x=144. These are background tiles. At y=144, the separately colored sprites are a red 8×8 square at x=16, a blue left-half 4×8 bar at x=80 and a green eight-row triangle at x=144. Final scrolling is (0,0).

The image checks 16,384 pixels for the expected shapes and colors, including sprite colors. Separate state tests cover 31 cases: register replacement, status/latch effects, saved scroll coordinates, zero/255-byte transfers, increments 1/32, map edges, zero rectangle dimensions, table selectors, whole-byte attributes and both palette targets. Values of Y=255 are checked as register writes, not as correct scrolling artwork. Evidence is from KUROSAKI with NROM; real hardware is not tested.

__ppu_addr

Evaluate ppu_addr once, read PPUSTATUS to reset the shared write latch, then write the high and low address bytes to PPUADDR. This sets the destination for later PPUDATA access without writing any data itself. The PPU applies its address mask and mirroring.

Syntax

c
void __ppu_addr(u16 ppu_addr);

Parameters

ppu_addr

PPU byte address (0x0000–0x3FFF), not a CPU pointer. The target must be writable: pattern changes need CHR RAM, not CHR ROM. PPU mapping and mirroring apply. Select increment 1 in PPUCTRL for contiguous copies and fills. Execute during safe PPU timing, then restore the desired scroll state; the executor writes PPUADDR and PPUDATA without restoring scroll settings.

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

Direct PPU access requires rendering to be off or the entire operation to fit a safe VBlank interval. These functions do not wait, queue, mask NMI or restore scroll. Prevent an interrupt from changing the shared latch/address during the call. PPUCTRL bit 2 selects a destination step of 1 or 32 per data byte. The PPU handles mirroring and address wrapping; CHR-ROM cannot be written. Set the intended scroll state after access and before rendering.

void PpuAddr(Expr e)
            {
                int[] t = AcquireTemps(2);
                try
                {
                    EmitLoadValue(e, ctx, 2);
                    EmitAsm("STA", Mem(t[0]));
                    EmitAsm("STX", Mem(t[1]));
                    EmitAsm("LDA", Mem(0x2002));
                    EmitAsm("LDA", Mem(t[1]));
                    EmitAsm("STA", Mem(0x2006));
                    EmitAsm("LDA", Mem(t[0]));
                    EmitAsm("STA", Mem(0x2006));
                }
                finally { ReleaseTemps(t); }
            }

At y=144, the separately colored sprites are a red 8×8 square at x=16, a blue left-half 4×8 bar at x=80 and a green eight-row triangle at x=144. Final scrolling is (0,0).

The image checks 16,384 pixels for the expected shapes and colors, including sprite colors. Separate state tests cover 31 cases: register replacement, status/latch effects, saved scroll coordinates, zero/255-byte transfers, increments 1/32, map edges, zero rectangle dimensions, table selectors, whole-byte attributes and both palette targets. Values of Y=255 are checked as register writes, not as correct scrolling artwork. Evidence is from KUROSAKI with NROM; real hardware is not tested.

__ppu_read_status

Read PPUSTATUS once and return the byte observed before the read clears its VBlank flag. The read also resets the shared scroll/address write latch. This is a hardware status read with side effects, not a cached frame counter or an NMI-completion test.

Syntax

c
u8 __ppu_read_status(void);

Return value

Raw status byte. Bit 7 is VBlank, bit 6 sprite-zero hit and bit 5 sprite overflow. Bits 0..4 retain the low bits of the PPU I/O latch, so they need not be zero. Test VBlank with (status & 0x80) != 0; a nonzero whole byte does not mean VBlank. These low bits are not application status or a frame counter.

Conditions and limits

A PPUSTATUS read can affect NMI timing and the next writes to both PPUSCROLL and PPUADDR. Do not insert it into another routine's half-written register pair. These calls do not wait for VBlank or complete pending transfer queues.

__prg_bank_set

Use the same mapper-aware PRG-bank selection as __bankswitch. This alias has the same bank validation and does not restore the previous mapping automatically.

Syntax

c
void __prg_bank_set(u8 bank);

Parameters

bank

An unsigned 8-bit ROM-bank number. For a call, it must agree with the function's placement; for a read, it selects the source mapping. Use the target cartridge's valid range.

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

A permanent bank change must not unmap the executing code or its return address. Put this call, bank_switch itself when used, and the code that continues afterwards in common/fixed bank 0, as the sample does.

The library record starts at zero and does not discover the cartridge's startup mapping. Initialize it with bank_switch. Direct intrinsics and raw mapper writes do not update this separate record; bank_get_current therefore cannot verify the actual hardware mapping.

FC switch-bank numbers are logical compiler numbers. Zero denotes common ROM, not a switch target. The helper normalizes zero to bank 1. On SUROM512, only 1–30 are valid: an out-of-range constant passed directly to the switching intrinsic is a build error; an invalid runtime value falls back to 1 and sets the mapper-fault state. Read common ROM directly instead of requesting a bank-zero switch.

Usage example

c
__prg_bank_set(1);bank_expect(home1[0]==0xA1,21);
__prg_bank_set(2); // Same mapper helper as __bankswitch.

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

The initial bank_switch(2) records and selects bank 2. Later, direct switching selects bank 1 and reads A1 from home1 while bank_get_current still reports 2; switching back makes home2 read B2 again.

The complete program teaches how a bank number and near address identify data, how callbacks cross banks, and how to distinguish the library's record from the actual mapping. All displayed numbers are hexadecimal. BANK IN and BANK OUT must show 02, BYTE HEX D3, WORD HEX 5C7A, and both FAILED CHECKS and FIRST FAILURE 00. CGB and FC display blue text; DMG displays black text.

CALL COUNT is 02: the far_call macro and __farcall each invoke the callback once.
