__rng8

Advance the shared 16-bit FC Galois LFSR once and return the XOR of the updated low and high bytes. An LFSR is a shift register whose feedback is calculated with XOR; a fixed seed therefore produces a reproducible byte sequence.

Syntax

c
u8 __rng8(void);

Return value

One u8 result (0–255), after advancing the shared generator once. This describes the value's type and bounds, not equal likelihood for every byte.

Conditions and limits

The FC step shifts the 16-bit state right by one. If the original least significant bit was 1, it XORs the shifted state with 0xB400. The returned byte is low_byte XOR high_byte, not the raw low byte.

If both state bytes are zero, the next draw substitutes 0xA55A before shifting. Thus __rng_seed(0) followed by __rng8() returns 255. The seed call stores zero; the substitution happens in the draw call.

These calls share persistent state. Reproduction requires the same target, seed and sequence of calls, including calls made by other helpers. Keep seed and draw operations in one execution context; these checks do not establish safe concurrent use from an interrupt handler.

GB and FC use different algorithms and do not promise the same sequence for the same seed. These are deterministic gameplay generators, not a source of cryptographic randomness; the tests check implementation behavior, not statistical quality or period.

Usage example

c
__rng_seed(0x1234);
first=__rng8();second=__rng8();third=__rng8(); // FC sequence: 19, 137, 240.

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

This sample reads three consecutive FC bytes. Seed 0x1234 produces FIRST 00019, SECOND 00137 and THIRD 00240. Those values show the call order; they are not a frequency or randomness score.

The complete NROM program prints blue decimal results on black. FAILED must read 00000. Text is uploaded with rendering disabled before the result screen is enabled.

Verification compared 32 outputs and eight subsequent byte draws per case with an independent host model: 93 GB cases and 18 FC cases, including constant/runtime seeds and GB range/chance/weight boundaries. The teaching screens were checked after 240 emulator frames. Physical hardware and statistical quality were not tested.

EmitHelperStart("__rng8");
            // 16-bit Galois LFSR: if low bit set, shift right then xor $B400.

__rob_flash

Select the on or off rendering mask and wait for one NMI-counter change. The selected mask remains in effect after return.

Syntax

c
void __rob_flash(u8 bright);

Parameters

bright

Zero selects off; any nonzero byte selects on, including 255. This is not a brightness level.

Return value

No return value. Return to the caller after the requested waits complete.

Conditions and limits

Include intrinsics.h. The default NMI handler must be running and advancing its counter. Disabled NMI or a custom handler that does not maintain that counter leaves the wait blocked. There is no timeout.

The on phase sets PPUMASK and its software shadow to 0x1E; the off phase sets both to zero. The previous mask is not restored. This changes background, sprite and left-edge rendering together and also replaces grayscale and color-emphasis settings.

Enabling rendering does not create a white screen by itself. Supply bright tiles and palette entries plus a dark backdrop for the off phase. The sample uses solid white tiles and a black backdrop, flashing the whole screen during the operation.

Wait counts measure NMI-counter changes. The interval from entry to the first NMI may be shorter than one frame. Call from foreground code, not an interrupt. Another routine changing the rendering mask can disturb the pattern.

These are low-level display-mask and wait primitives. They do not generate a robot command preamble, device-specific command sequence or reception acknowledgement. Verification covers PPUMASK writes, NMI counts and pixels in KUROSAKI; physical robot reception has not been tested.

Usage example

c
start=__nmi_ready();
    __rob_flash(1); // Enable rendering and wait for one NMI-counter change.
    rob_result[0]=(u8)(__nmi_ready()-start);
    __rob_flash(0); // Disable rendering; the black backdrop remains visible.

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

After execution, the screen shows FLASH WAITS 1, PULSE 3 ON / 2 OFF = 5 and A5 BYTE WAITS 48. The diagram represents 0xA5: 1,0,1,0 on the upper row and 0,1,0,1 below. Each cell is one wait; white means rendering enabled and black means disabled. A one has four white cells followed by two black cells; a zero has two white followed by four black. FINAL MASK 0 and TIMING CHECKS OK indicate completion.

__rob_pulse

Perform the requested on waits followed by the requested off waits, producing one pulse.

Syntax

c
void __rob_pulse(u8 on_frames, u8 off_frames);

Parameters

on_frames

On-phase wait count, 0..255. Zero skips the on phase.

off_frames

Off-phase wait count, 0..255. Zero skips the off phase. The total can reach 510 waits.

Return value

No return value. Return to the caller after the requested waits complete.

Conditions and limits

With both counts zero, neither the mask nor timing changes. Any off waits leave mask zero; an on-only pulse leaves 0x1E.

Include intrinsics.h. The default NMI handler must be running and advancing its counter. Disabled NMI or a custom handler that does not maintain that counter leaves the wait blocked. There is no timeout.

The on phase sets PPUMASK and its software shadow to 0x1E; the off phase sets both to zero. The previous mask is not restored. This changes background, sprite and left-edge rendering together and also replaces grayscale and color-emphasis settings.

Enabling rendering does not create a white screen by itself. Supply bright tiles and palette entries plus a dark backdrop for the off phase. The sample uses solid white tiles and a black backdrop, flashing the whole screen during the operation.

Wait counts measure NMI-counter changes. The interval from entry to the first NMI may be shorter than one frame. Call from foreground code, not an interrupt. Another routine changing the rendering mask can disturb the pattern.

These are low-level display-mask and wait primitives. They do not generate a robot command preamble, device-specific command sequence or reception acknowledgement. Verification covers PPUMASK writes, NMI counts and pixels in KUROSAKI; physical robot reception has not been tested.

Usage example

c
start=__nmi_ready();
    __rob_pulse(3,2); // Three enabled waits, then two disabled waits.
    rob_result[1]=(u8)(__nmi_ready()-start);

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

After execution, the screen shows FLASH WAITS 1, PULSE 3 ON / 2 OFF = 5 and A5 BYTE WAITS 48. The diagram represents 0xA5: 1,0,1,0 on the upper row and 0,1,0,1 below. Each cell is one wait; white means rendering enabled and black means disabled. A one has four white cells followed by two black cells; a zero has two white followed by four black. FINAL MASK 0 and TIMING CHECKS OK indicate completion.

__rob_send_byte

Encode one byte as eight blink patterns, most-significant bit first. One uses four on waits and two off waits; zero uses two on waits and four off waits. The total is 48 NMI waits.

Syntax

c
void __rob_send_byte(u8 pattern);

Parameters

pattern

Eight-bit pattern, 0..255. For 0xA5 the order is 1,0,1,0,0,1,0,1. This is not a channel ID or a robot action number.

Return value

No return value. Return to the caller after the requested waits complete.

Conditions and limits

The last bit also ends with off waits, leaving PPUMASK and its shadow at zero. Send exactly eight bits; no start or end marker is added.

Include intrinsics.h. The default NMI handler must be running and advancing its counter. Disabled NMI or a custom handler that does not maintain that counter leaves the wait blocked. There is no timeout.

The on phase sets PPUMASK and its software shadow to 0x1E; the off phase sets both to zero. The previous mask is not restored. This changes background, sprite and left-edge rendering together and also replaces grayscale and color-emphasis settings.

Enabling rendering does not create a white screen by itself. Supply bright tiles and palette entries plus a dark backdrop for the off phase. The sample uses solid white tiles and a black backdrop, flashing the whole screen during the operation.

Wait counts measure NMI-counter changes. The interval from entry to the first NMI may be shorter than one frame. Call from foreground code, not an interrupt. Another routine changing the rendering mask can disturb the pattern.

These are low-level display-mask and wait primitives. They do not generate a robot command preamble, device-specific command sequence or reception acknowledgement. Verification covers PPUMASK writes, NMI counts and pixels in KUROSAKI; physical robot reception has not been tested.

Usage example

c
start=__nmi_ready();
    __rob_send_byte(0xA5); // 10100101, most-significant bit first; 48 waits.
    rob_result[2]=(u8)(__nmi_ready()-start);
    rob_result[3]=__ppu_mask_get(); // Zero: the sequence ends with rendering off.

Each cell is one wait; white means rendering enabled and black means disabled. A one has four white cells followed by two black cells; a zero has two white followed by four black. FINAL MASK 0 and TIMING CHECKS OK indicate completion.

__scroll_latch_reset

Read PPUSTATUS and discard the result to reset the shared PPU scroll/address write latch. It also clears the VBlank flag. No zero scroll coordinates are written, and saved X/Y values are not changed.

Syntax

c
void __scroll_latch_reset(void);

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

A PPUSTATUS read can affect NMI timing and the next writes to both PPUSCROLL and PPUADDR. Do not insert it into another routine's half-written register pair. These calls do not wait for VBlank or complete pending transfer queues.

NESdev: PPU registers

NESdev: PPU scrolling

Usage example

c
address_port=0x21; // Leave the shared latch halfway through an address pair.
__scroll_latch_reset();
address_port=0x21;address_port=0x83;data_port=2; // Blue left-half marker.

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

This program teaches register setup, direct tile/attribute writes, scrolling and separate background/sprite palette loads. The blue band at (0,16) measures 256×16 pixels: its first row repeats a solid 8×8 tile, a left-half 4×8 bar and an eight-row triangle; its second row contains only left-half bars. A solid green 64×32 rectangle starts at (16,48). A red 64×32 region at (144,48) contains an 8-by-4 grid of triangle tiles.

At y=96, blue markers at x=16, 24 and 32 are respectively a square, left-half bar and triangle; a red left-half bar is at x=80 and a green triangle at x=144. These are background tiles. At y=144, the separately colored sprites are a red 8×8 square at x=16, a blue left-half 4×8 bar at x=80 and a green eight-row triangle at x=144. Final scrolling is (0,0).

The image checks 16,384 pixels for the expected shapes and colors, including sprite colors. Separate state tests cover 31 cases: register replacement, status/latch effects, saved scroll coordinates, zero/255-byte transfers, increments 1/32, map edges, zero rectangle dimensions, table selectors, whole-byte attributes and both palette targets. Values of Y=255 are checked as register writes, not as correct scrolling artwork. Evidence is from KUROSAKI with NROM; real hardware is not tested.

__scroll_set

Save both pixel offsets in the runtime X/Y shadows, read PPUSTATUS to reset the shared latch, then write X and Y to PPUSCROLL in that order. This updates scrolling immediately; it does not queue a camera move, wait for NMI or choose a base nametable.

Syntax

c
void __scroll_set(u8 x, u8 y);

Parameters

x / y

Offsets are unsigned pixel bytes. Use X 0..255 and normally Y 0..239; Y 240..255 is written unchanged but has special PPU row behavior, not ordinary visible-map scrolling. PPUCTRL supplies the base nametable bits. Restore intended scrolling after direct VRAM access and before rendering; the function does not schedule that timing for you.

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

A PPUSTATUS read can affect NMI timing and the next writes to both PPUSCROLL and PPUADDR. Do not insert it into another routine's half-written register pair. These calls do not wait for VBlank or complete pending transfer queues.

__sdot2_q1_7

Compute a signed two-term dot product.

Syntax

c
u16 __sdot2_q1_7(u16 a0, u16 a1, u8 b0, u8 b1);

Parameters

a0

Signed 16-bit bit pattern, representing −32768..32767.

a1

Signed 16-bit bit pattern, representing −32768..32767.

b0

Signed byte bit pattern, coefficient −128..127.

b1

Signed byte bit pattern, coefficient −128..127.

Return value

Returns the low 16 bits of a0*b0+a1*b1.

Conditions and limits

On FC, q8_8/q1_7 names still use raw integer products without a fixed-point downshift. The Q1.7 functions alias their corresponding signed operations. The caller handles units; signed results are returned as u16 bit patterns.

Usage example

c
// Compare literal coefficients with values read from RAM.
result[34]=__sdot2_q1_7(-513,769,-64,127);
v0=-513;v1=769;v2=-64;v3=127;
result[35]=__sdot2_q1_7(v0,v1,v2,v3);
// Reverse coefficient signs and verify negative products.
result[36]=__sdot2_q1_7(-513,769,64,-127);
v0=-513;v1=769;v2=64;v3=-127;
result[37]=__sdot2_q1_7(v0,v1,v2,v3);

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

Compare literal inputs with values stored in RAM. Representative results appear as unsigned 16-bit values; negatives use two’s-complement bit patterns. GB rescales fixed-point products, while FC returns integer products, so identical inputs need not give identical results.

The excerpt stores these 16-bit values: result[34]=64959, result[35]=64959, result[36]=577, result[37]=577. Each literal-input calculation matches its RAM-input counterpart. The screen shows representative values; the result array holds every result.

void EmitHelperMath()
        {
            // Consume eight multiplier bits and accumulate the low product word in shared temporaries, returning A/X.
            EmitHelperStart("__mul16x8");
            EmitAsm("LDA", Imm(0));
            EmitAsm("STA", Mem(_runtimeIntrinsicTmp0Address));
            EmitAsm("STA", Mem(_runtimeIntrinsicTmp1Address));
            EmitAsm("LDX", Imm(8));
            string loop = NewGeneratedLabel("mul16x8_loop");
            string skip = NewGeneratedLabel("mul16x8_skip_add");
            _assembly.Add(Expr.Make(Tag.Label, loop));
            EmitAsm("LSR", Mem(CallArgBase + 2));
            EmitAsm("BCC", Rel(skip));
            EmitAsm("LDA", Mem(_runtimeIntrinsicTmp0Address));
            EmitAsm("CLC");
            EmitAsm("ADC", Mem(CallArgBase));
            EmitAsm("STA", Mem(_runtimeIntrinsicTmp0Address));
            EmitAsm("LDA", Mem(_runtimeIntrinsicTmp1Address));
            EmitAsm("ADC", Mem(CallArgBase + 1));
            EmitAsm("STA", Mem(_runtimeIntrinsicTmp1Address));

__sdot2_q8_8

Compute a signed two-term dot product.

Syntax

c
u16 __sdot2_q8_8(u16 a0, u16 a1, u8 b0, u8 b1);

Parameters

a0

Signed 16-bit bit pattern, representing −32768..32767.

a1

Signed 16-bit bit pattern, representing −32768..32767.

b0

Signed byte bit pattern, coefficient −128..127.

b1

Signed byte bit pattern, coefficient −128..127.

Return value

Returns the low 16 bits of a0*b0+a1*b1.

Conditions and limits

On FC, q8_8/q1_7 names still use raw integer products without a fixed-point downshift. The Q1.7 functions alias their corresponding signed operations. The caller handles units; signed results are returned as u16 bit patterns.

Usage example

c
// Compare literal coefficients with values read from RAM.
result[26]=__sdot2_q8_8(-513,769,-64,127);
v0=-513;v1=769;v2=-64;v3=127;
result[27]=__sdot2_q8_8(v0,v1,v2,v3);
// Reverse coefficient signs and verify negative products.
result[28]=__sdot2_q8_8(-513,769,64,-127);
v0=-513;v1=769;v2=64;v3=-127;
result[29]=__sdot2_q8_8(v0,v1,v2,v3);

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

Compare literal inputs with values stored in RAM. Representative results appear as unsigned 16-bit values; negatives use two’s-complement bit patterns. GB rescales fixed-point products, while FC returns integer products, so identical inputs need not give identical results.

The excerpt stores these 16-bit values: result[26]=64959, result[27]=64959, result[28]=577, result[29]=577. Each literal-input calculation matches its RAM-input counterpart. The screen shows representative values; the result array holds every result.

Complete example program

Build command

powershell
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force .\out | Out-Null
.\kitaqfc\kitaqfc.exe .\kitaq-docs\samples\api-examples\fc\batch3_math.c -I .\kitaqfc\lib -I .\kitaq-docs\samples -o .\out\batch3_math.nes --no-cache --no-disasm --mapper=nrom --nes-chr=.\kitaq-docs\samples\font.chr

__serial_rx_bit

Sample $4017 bit 4 once as the receive line supplied by an external adapter.

Syntax

c
u8 __serial_rx_bit(void);

Return value

1 when bit 4 is set, otherwise 0. This is not a data-ready or communication-error status.

Conditions and limits

These APIs access $4016/$4017 directly. Do not interleave interrupt-driven gamepad, keyboard or serial operations on the same ports. Controller shift positions can also be affected. The sample disables NMI while capturing input, then enables it when initializing the display.

These low-level primitives assume an external adapter mapping OUT0 to TX and $4017 D4 to RX. They add no bit interval, baud clock, start/stop bits, byte assembly or receive wait. Their role differs from byte-oriented helpers such as __midi_out().

The caller must sample at the appropriate time. This neither waits for data nor assembles multiple bits, and it does not change the $4016 output.

Bit conversion is also unit-tested in an owned test ROM by redirecting register reads to RAM fixture values. The tests cover 00/08/10/18 combinations with unrelated bits set. This unit test is separate from the unmodified sample run and from real peripheral behavior.

These images run the downloadable ROMs unchanged in KUROSAKI. Its current input bus models gamepads but not keyboard, light-gun or serial-adapter signals. The external input bits read as zero, so the captures do not verify those devices. Physical key input, optical sensing and communication remain untested.

Usage example

c
#include "fc_ports_scene.h"
__prg_rom u8 tx_values[6]={0,1,2,3,254,255};
void main(void){
    u8 i;
    __irq_disable();__ppu_ctrl_set(0);port_phase=1;
    for(i=0;i<6;i++)__serial_tx_bit(tx_values[i]);
    __serial_tx_bit(1); // Leave OUT0 high; no byte framing or baud clock is added.
    port_result[0]=__serial_rx_bit();port_phase=2;port_result[31]=165;
    m_init();m_text(2,2,"SERIAL BIT PRIMITIVES");m_wait();
    m_text(2,5,"VALUE       EXPECTED OUT0");m_wait();
    for(i=0;i<6;i++){port_number(3,7+i*2,tx_values[i]);m_put(23,7+i*2,'0'+(tx_values[i]&1));m_wait();}
    m_text(2,20,"RX SAMPLE");port_number(23,20,port_result[0]);m_wait();
    m_text(2,23,"NO BYTE FRAMING OR CLOCK");m_wait();
    while(1){m_wait();}
}

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

For VALUE 000/001/002/003/254/255, EXPECTED OUT0 is 0/1/0/1/0/1. This column explains the low-bit mapping; it is not electrical readback. CPU traces confirm those writes followed by a final one. RX SAMPLE is 000 because KUROSAKI does not model the receive line.

.\kurosaki\kurosaki.exe run .\out\peripheral_serial.nes --frames 120 --png .\out\peripheral_serial.png

__serial_tx_bit

Write the argument’s low bit to OUT0 through $4016, providing a one-bit output operation for an external serial adapter.

Syntax

c
void __serial_tx_bit(u8 bit);

Parameters

bit

Value to output. Only bit & 1 is used: 2 outputs zero, while 255 outputs one.

Return value

No return value.

Conditions and limits

These APIs access $4016/$4017 directly. Do not interleave interrupt-driven gamepad, keyboard or serial operations on the same ports. Controller shift positions can also be affected. The sample disables NMI while capturing input, then enables it when initializing the display.

These low-level primitives assume an external adapter mapping OUT0 to TX and $4017 D4 to RX. They add no bit interval, baud clock, start/stop bits, byte assembly or receive wait. Their role differs from byte-oriented helpers such as __midi_out().

Writes the entire $4016 value as zero or one, clearing OUT1/OUT2. No hold delay is inserted. OUT0 controls the normal gamepad latch, so this operation changes gamepad reading state too.

These images run the downloadable ROMs unchanged in KUROSAKI. Its current input bus models gamepads but not keyboard, light-gun or serial-adapter signals. The external input bits read as zero, so the captures do not verify those devices. Physical key input, optical sensing and communication remain untested.

R.O.B. / Famicom Robot optical flash primitives. These are timing primitives;
game-specific command sequences should be built on top of __rob_pulse() or
__rob_send_byte().
/
Set PPUMASK and its shadow to 1E or 00, then wait for an NMI-counter change.
The caller supplies image/palette brightness; rendering enable alone does not create a white screen.
void __rob_flash(u8 bright);
Run on_frames enabled-mask waits followed by off_frames disabled-mask waits; NMI must advance.
void __rob_pulse(u8 on_frames, u8 off_frames);
Send eight bits MSB first: one uses 4 on/2 off waits; zero uses 2 on/4 off.
Requires an advancing runtime NMI counter; 48 waits in total, final PPUMASK=0.
This raw pattern does not add a robot command preamble or validate reception.
void __rob_send_byte(u8 pattern);

 Expansion-port TTL serial / MIDI adapter support.
The low-level serial layer assumes an external adapter that maps OUT0 to TX
and D4 on $4017 to RX. MIDI helpers bit-bang 8N1 bytes at an approximate
31250 bps timing suitable for adapter bring-up and simple music sync.
/
Write bit & 1 to 4016, replacing the port output value; coordinate with other port users.

__smac16

Compute a signed multiply-accumulate.

Syntax

c
u16 __smac16(u16 acc, u16 a, u8 b);

Parameters

acc

16-bit accumulator to add.

a

Signed 16-bit bit pattern, representing −32768..32767.

b

Signed byte bit pattern, coefficient −128..127.

Return value

Returns the low 16 bits of acc+a*b.

Conditions and limits

On FC, q8_8/q1_7 names still use raw integer products without a fixed-point downshift. The Q1.7 functions alias their corresponding signed operations. The caller handles units; signed results are returned as u16 bit patterns.

Usage example

c
// Compare literal coefficients with values read from RAM.
result[10]=__smac16(65500,-513,-64);
v0=65500;v1=-513;v2=-64;
result[11]=__smac16(v0,v1,v2);
// Reverse coefficient signs and verify negative products.
result[12]=__smac16(65500,-513,64);
v0=65500;v1=-513;v2=64;
result[13]=__smac16(v0,v1,v2);

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

Compare literal inputs with values stored in RAM. Representative results appear as unsigned 16-bit values; negatives use two’s-complement bit patterns. GB rescales fixed-point products, while FC returns integer products, so identical inputs need not give identical results.

The excerpt stores these 16-bit values: result[10]=32796, result[11]=32796, result[12]=32668, result[13]=32668. Each literal-input calculation matches its RAM-input counterpart. The screen shows representative values; the result array holds every result.

Compute a signed multiplication.

Syntax

c
u16 __smul16x8(u16 a, u8 b);

Parameters

a

Signed 16-bit bit pattern, representing −32768..32767.

b

Signed byte bit pattern, coefficient −128..127.

Return value

Returns the low 16 bits of a*b.

Conditions and limits

On FC, q8_8/q1_7 names still use raw integer products without a fixed-point downshift. The Q1.7 functions alias their corresponding signed operations. The caller handles units; signed results are returned as u16 bit patterns.

Usage example

c
// Compare literal coefficients with values read from RAM.

v0=-513;v1=-64;
result[5]=__smul16x8(v0,v1);
// Reverse coefficient signs and verify negative products.
result[6]=__smul16x8(-513,64);
v0=-513;v1=64;
result[7]=__smul16x8(v0,v1);

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

Compare literal inputs with values stored in RAM. Representative results appear as unsigned 16-bit values; negatives use two’s-complement bit patterns. GB rescales fixed-point products, while FC returns integer products, so identical inputs need not give identical results.

The excerpt stores these 16-bit values: result[4]=32832, result[5]=32832, result[6]=32704, result[7]=32704. Each literal-input calculation matches its RAM-input counterpart. The screen shows representative values; the result array holds every result.

__split_scroll_sprite0

Wait for a fresh sprite-zero hit and write scroll X/Y for a horizontal split, keeping the top aligned while shifting the lower background.

Syntax

c
void __split_scroll_sprite0(u8 x, u8 y);

Parameters

x

Horizontal scroll value, 0..255, not an object’s screen X coordinate. The sample uses 32 to display the lower part of the same background shifted left by 32 pixels.

y

Temporary vertical scroll setting, 0..255; the usual visible range is 0..239. This helper writes $2005, so it does not immediately change the live vertical position during rendering. The horizontal-split sample passes zero.

Return value

No return value.

Conditions and limits

Overlap an opaque pixel of OAM sprite 0 with an opaque background pixel, with both layers enabled. The behind-background priority flag still permits a hit. The leftmost eight pixels require the corresponding layer enables; overlap at X=255 cannot trigger a hit.

Poll PPUSTATUS ($2002) bit 6 until it is clear, then until it is set. If a hit has already occurred when called, wait for a fresh hit in the next frame. Reading the flag does not acknowledge it; the PPU clears it during pre-render.

There is no timeout or failure return. A hidden sprite 0, transparent background, disabled rendering or another setup without overlap leaves the call blocked. Guarantee a hit before calling. CPU IRQ enable is not required, and this function does not enable NMI. The sample enables NMI for its separate frame wait.

Reads of $2002 also affect the shared PPU address/scroll write latch and the VBlank flag. Do not split a two-write $2005/$2006 operation around this call. Use it from the foreground, not from an NMI/IRQ handler.

After the hit, read $2002 and write X then Y to $2005. Fine X changes immediately; coarse X takes effect at the next horizontal reload. Y normally takes effect at the next pre-render reload, unless another scroll write replaces it first. This is not an immediate arbitrary-X/Y raster repositioning operation.

Polling and instruction execution delay the writes. KUROSAKI renders by scanline, so these captures do not establish a dot-exact hardware boundary. The sample places the change inside the white band at Y=96..103, keeping boundary uncertainty away from the blue and red bars.

The shared header fc_sprite0_scene.h prepares original blue/red bars and a white horizontal band. Sprite 0 sits at screen (16,96), hidden behind the background; its raw OAM Y is 95 because display Y is OAM Y+1. Each frame restores the top scroll to zero during VBlank before waiting for the hit.

NESdev: PPU scrolling

NESdev: PPU programmer reference

Usage example

c
void main(void) {
    s0_prepare();
    while (1) {
        s0_frame();
        __split_scroll_sprite0(32,0);
        s0_completed++;
    }
}

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

Above the white band, blue is at X=64..95 and red at X=160..191. Below it, from Y=104 onward, blue moves to X=32..63 and red to X=128..159: only the lower area shifts left by 32 pixels. The horizontal band is at Y=96..103 and the bars end at Y=207. Verification checks one completion per frame and every image pixel’s position and color.

__sprite_attr

Replace the complete attribute byte of one shadow sprite. Use it to choose the palette, set background priority, or flip the pattern horizontally or vertically without changing its tile or position.

Syntax

c
void __sprite_attr(u8 index, u8 attr);

Parameters

index

Sprite entry number, 0–63, not a byte offset. The implementation multiplies it by four using an 8-bit cursor; out-of-range values wrap modulo 64 and can overwrite another entry. No allocation check is performed.

attr

Complete attribute byte: bits 0–1 select sprite palette 0–3; bit 5 places opaque sprite pixels behind opaque background pixels; bits 6 and 7 flip horizontally and vertically. Keep bits 2–4 zero. Combine flags with bitwise OR; the supplied byte replaces all previous attributes.

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

These operations edit CPU RAM at 0x0200–0x02FF; they do not immediately change hardware OAM. Transfer the completed page with __oam_dma. They do not maintain the sprite library’s allocation flags, coordinate arrays or active count. Keep interrupt handlers from editing or transferring a partially prepared page.

Usage example

c
__sprite_attr(3,0xC0); // Flip the arrow horizontally and vertically.

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

The example separates each operation into a labeled row. SET and MOVE show 8×8 right arrows at (144,16) and (144,32); TILE shows a green square at (144,48); ATTR shows the arrow flipped both ways at (144,64). HIDE at (144,80) and CLEAR at (144,112) must stay empty. META shows a pair at (136,96) and (144,96), with the second arrow mirrored horizontally. NEXT 07 is the next write position after writing slots 5 and 6. Arrows have red edges, green shafts and blue tip details. Verification compares 8,704 pixels per image and checks the transferred OAM bytes; physical hardware is untested.

TRANSFER shows an arrow at (144,128). This program sends page 02 directly with __oam_dma, including every field prepared by the individual sprite operations.

__sprite_move

Change only the X and Y bytes of one shadow sprite. Its tile number and attributes stay intact, so the same graphic moves without changing its palette or flips.

Syntax

c
void __sprite_move(u8 index, u8 x, u8 y);

Parameters

index

Sprite entry number, 0–63, not a byte offset. The implementation multiplies it by four using an 8-bit cursor; out-of-range values wrap modulo 64 and can overwrite another entry. No allocation check is performed.

x

Horizontal position in pixels, stored as an unsigned byte. This is a pixel coordinate, not a tile coordinate.

y

Raw OAM Y byte. Use visible_top-1 for a visible top below scanline zero; values 239..255 are outside the visible 240-line area.

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

These operations edit CPU RAM at 0x0200–0x02FF; they do not immediately change hardware OAM. Transfer the completed page with __oam_dma. They do not maintain the sprite library’s allocation flags, coordinate arrays or active count. Keep interrupt handlers from editing or transferring a partially prepared page.

Usage example

c
__sprite_move(1,144,31); // Move to (144,32), retaining tile 128 and attributes 0.

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

The example separates each operation into a labeled row. SET and MOVE show 8×8 right arrows at (144,16) and (144,32); TILE shows a green square at (144,48); ATTR shows the arrow flipped both ways at (144,64). HIDE at (144,80) and CLEAR at (144,112) must stay empty. META shows a pair at (136,96) and (144,96), with the second arrow mirrored horizontally. NEXT 07 is the next write position after writing slots 5 and 6. Arrows have red edges, green shafts and blue tip details. Verification compares 8,704 pixels per image and checks the transferred OAM bytes; physical hardware is untested.

TRANSFER shows an arrow at (144,128). This program sends page 02 directly with __oam_dma, including every field prepared by the individual sprite operations.

__sprite_set

Write all four fields of one sprite into the page-02 shadow buffer. Arguments are index, X, Y, tile and attributes; the stored byte order is Y, tile, attributes, X.

Syntax

c
void __sprite_set(u8 index, u8 x, u8 y, u8 tile, u8 attr);

Parameters

index

Sprite entry number, 0–63, not a byte offset. The implementation multiplies it by four using an 8-bit cursor; out-of-range values wrap modulo 64 and can overwrite another entry. No allocation check is performed.

x

Horizontal position in pixels, stored as an unsigned byte. This is a pixel coordinate, not a tile coordinate.

y

Raw OAM Y byte. Use visible_top-1 for a visible top below scanline zero; values 239..255 are outside the visible 240-line area.

tile

Eight-bit tile number. Load its graphics first. Hardware rules for 8×16 sprites still apply; this function does not adjust the number for paired tiles.

attr

Complete attribute byte: bits 0–1 select sprite palette 0–3; bit 5 places opaque sprite pixels behind opaque background pixels; bits 6 and 7 flip horizontally and vertically. Keep bits 2–4 zero. Combine flags with bitwise OR; the supplied byte replaces all previous attributes.

__vram_fill

Set ppu_addr, then write the same byte value to PPUDATA exactly len times. This is a direct fill, completed before return. It does not interpret tile dimensions, attributes or rectangular boundaries.

Syntax

c
void __vram_fill(u16 ppu_addr, u8 value, u8 len);

Parameters

ppu_addr

PPU byte address (0x0000–0x3FFF), not a CPU pointer. The target must be writable: pattern changes need CHR RAM, not CHR ROM. PPU mapping and mirroring apply. Select increment 1 in PPUCTRL for contiguous copies and fills. Execute during safe PPU timing, then restore the desired scroll state; the executor writes PPUADDR and PPUDATA without restoring scroll settings.

value

One byte, 0–255, written repeatedly. Its visible meaning depends on whether the destination contains tile indices, pixel planes or another byte-based structure.

len

Number of bytes, 0..255. Zero still sets the PPU address and resets the latch, but writes no data. There is no destination-capacity check, clipping, bank switch or deferred transfer.

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

Direct PPU access requires rendering to be off or the entire operation to fit a safe VBlank interval. These functions do not wait, queue, mask NMI or restore scroll. Prevent an interrupt from changing the shared latch/address during the call. PPUCTRL bit 2 selects a destination step of 1 or 32 per data byte. The PPU handles mirroring and address wrapping; CHR-ROM cannot be written. Set the intended scroll state after access and before rendering.

NESdev: PPU registers

NESdev: PPU scrolling

Usage example

c
__vram_fill(0x2060,2,32); // A second blue row of 4-pixel-wide left halves.

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

This program teaches register setup, direct tile/attribute writes, scrolling and separate background/sprite palette loads. The blue band at (0,16) measures 256×16 pixels: its first row repeats a solid 8×8 tile, a left-half 4×8 bar and an eight-row triangle; its second row contains only left-half bars. A solid green 64×32 rectangle starts at (16,48). A red 64×32 region at (144,48) contains an 8-by-4 grid of triangle tiles.

At y=96, blue markers at x=16, 24 and 32 are respectively a square, left-half bar and triangle; a red left-half bar is at x=80 and a green triangle at x=144. These are background tiles. At y=144, the separately colored sprites are a red 8×8 square at x=16, a blue left-half 4×8 bar at x=80 and a green eight-row triangle at x=144. Final scrolling is (0,0).

The image checks 16,384 pixels for the expected shapes and colors, including sprite colors. Separate state tests cover 31 cases: register replacement, status/latch effects, saved scroll coordinates, zero/255-byte transfers, increments 1/32, map edges, zero rectangle dimensions, table selectors, whole-byte attributes and both palette targets. Values of Y=255 are checked as register writes, not as correct scrolling artwork. Evidence is from KUROSAKI with NROM; real hardware is not tested.

__vram_write

Reset the PPU latch, set ppu_addr and synchronously copy len consecutive source bytes to PPUDATA. The count is eight-bit; the compiler uses indexed source reads. No pointer is retained for later execution, and changing the source after return does not change VRAM.

Syntax

c
void __vram_write(u16 ppu_addr, const u8* src, u8 len);

Parameters

ppu_addr

PPU byte address (0x0000–0x3FFF), not a CPU pointer. The target must be writable: pattern changes need CHR RAM, not CHR ROM. PPU mapping and mirroring apply. Select increment 1 in PPUCTRL for contiguous copies and fills. Execute during safe PPU timing, then restore the desired scroll state; the executor writes PPUADDR and PPUDATA without restoring scroll settings.

src

CPU pointer to at least the requested number of readable bytes. Keep the source mapped and stable until this synchronous transfer returns. There is no bank switching, retained queue pointer or source-length check; a zero count does not dereference the pointer.

len

Number of bytes, 0..255. Zero still sets the PPU address and resets the latch, but writes no data. There is no destination-capacity check, clipping, bank switch or deferred transfer.

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

Direct PPU access requires rendering to be off or the entire operation to fit a safe VBlank interval. These functions do not wait, queue, mask NMI or restore scroll. Prevent an interrupt from changing the shared latch/address during the call. PPUCTRL bit 2 selects a destination step of 1 or 32 per data byte. The PPU handles mirroring and address wrapping; CHR-ROM cannot be written. Set the intended scroll state after access and before rendering.

__vramq_capacity

Return the total capacity of the command buffer, regardless of how much is currently used.

Syntax

c
u8 __vramq_capacity(void);

Return value

An unsigned byte in the platform-specific units described here. Reading it does not modify or execute the queue.

Conditions and limits

FC counts bytes of encoded commands in a fixed 128-byte intrinsic buffer. A tile write costs 4 bytes, a fill record 5 and a pointer-copy record 6, including metadata. A ready queue can be consumed by NMI; inspect or build it before committing, and coordinate the producer with the consumer.

These intrinsics operate on the same command buffer used by lib/vram.c. The nes_vram_queue_* functions in runtime.c manage a separate queue with a different record format. Clearing or querying one does not clear or measure the other.

Build and consume the queue in coordinated phases. Do not append while an interrupt executes it, change its bookkeeping directly, or overwrite retained source data unintentionally. These APIs provide neither locking nor double buffering. Capacity describes the command buffer, not free bytes in hardware VRAM.

Usage example

c
capacity=__vramq_capacity();
if (capacity!=128) failures++;

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

The complete program teaches queue capacity, retained pointers, independent reset flags and immediate versus NMI execution. Expect CAPACITY 128, ENCODED BYTES 030, AFTER EXEC 000, OVERFLOW SEEN 001 and FAILED CHECKS 000. Six records use 30 buffer bytes but perform 512 byte writes. OVERFLOW SEEN preserves the earlier intentional rejection; it is not a claim that the final latch remains set.

The blue copy starts at pixel (0,16), and the green fill at (0,88). Each covers seven full 256-pixel rows of tiles, then 248 pixels of the eighth tile row: 255 tiles total. The final 8 × 8 cell stays black. The copy repeats solid, left-half and triangular 8 × 8 patterns; its first tile is a triangle because the source changed after enqueueing. The fill stays solid even after its caller variable changes. Both shape and color are checked.

At y=160, expect a red solid square at x=16, a red left-half tile at x=224 and a red solid square at x=240. The first survives zero-length copy/fill records; the middle proves default-NMI consumption; the last is a single put. The cancelled cell at (248,160) must remain black. The long transfers run with rendering and NMI off; only the final small write uses NMI. This is NROM emulator evidence, not a real-hardware test.

__vramq_commit

Set the queue's ready flag to 1 so the executor may consume it. This does not copy payloads, execute PPU writes or wait for NMI. Once committed, keep the queue and retained sources stable until execution finishes. With NMI enabled, the default handler can consume it asynchronously.

Syntax

c
void __vramq_commit(void);

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

FC counts bytes of encoded commands in a fixed 128-byte intrinsic buffer. A tile write costs 4 bytes, a fill record 5 and a pointer-copy record 6, including metadata. A ready queue can be consumed by NMI; inspect or build it before committing, and coordinate the producer with the consumer.

These intrinsics operate on the same command buffer used by lib/vram.c. The nes_vram_queue_* functions in runtime.c manage a separate queue with a different record format. Clearing or querying one does not clear or measure the other.

Build and consume the queue in coordinated phases. Do not append while an interrupt executes it, change its bookkeeping directly, or overwrite retained source data unintentionally. These APIs provide neither locking nor double buffering. Capacity describes the command buffer, not free bytes in hardware VRAM.

Usage example

c
__vramq_commit(); // NMI is disabled here: this only marks the queue ready.
if (__vramq_len()!=30) failures++;

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

The complete program teaches queue capacity, retained pointers, independent reset flags and immediate versus NMI execution. Expect CAPACITY 128, ENCODED BYTES 030, AFTER EXEC 000, OVERFLOW SEEN 001 and FAILED CHECKS 000. Six records use 30 buffer bytes but perform 512 byte writes. OVERFLOW SEEN preserves the earlier intentional rejection; it is not a claim that the final latch remains set.

The blue copy starts at pixel (0,16), and the green fill at (0,88). Each covers seven full 256-pixel rows of tiles, then 248 pixels of the eighth tile row: 255 tiles total. The final 8 × 8 cell stays black. The copy repeats solid, left-half and triangular 8 × 8 patterns; its first tile is a triangle because the source changed after enqueueing. The fill stays solid even after its caller variable changes. Both shape and color are checked.

At y=160, expect a red solid square at x=16, a red left-half tile at x=224 and a red solid square at x=240. The first survives zero-length copy/fill records; the middle proves default-NMI consumption; the last is a single put. The cancelled cell at (248,160) must remain black. The long transfers run with rendering and NMI off; only the final small write uses NMI. This is NROM emulator evidence, not a real-hardware test.

kitaqfc/lib/intrinsics.h:150

Declaration notes (original source)
Publish the pending records to the configured consumer. Do not mutate them while consumption can run.
__vramq_copy

Append one six-byte record that copies len bytes from src to ppu_addr at execution time. The queue retains the source pointer, not the payload. A 255-byte copy still occupies only six command-buffer bytes. Bytes are streamed in increasing source order; select PPU increment 1 for a contiguous destination.

Syntax

c
void __vramq_copy(u16 ppu_addr, const u8* src, u8 len);

Parameters

ppu_addr

PPU byte address (0x0000–0x3FFF), not a CPU pointer. The target must be writable: pattern changes need CHR RAM, not CHR ROM. PPU mapping and mirroring apply. Select increment 1 in PPUCTRL for contiguous copies and fills. Execute during safe PPU timing, then restore the desired scroll state; the executor writes PPUADDR and PPUDATA without restoring scroll settings.

src

Near pointer to readable bytes, retained until execution. Keep the required bytes alive and their memory/ROM bank mapped for the entire flush; no bank number or payload copy is stored. A nonempty transfer requires a valid source. Do not use an expired local array.

len

Number of bytes, from 0 to 255. One record handles the full count; it is not split into 127-byte chunks. Zero still occupies a copy/fill record. On execution, a zero count sets the PPU address but writes no PPUDATA bytes. A value of 256 is outside this argument's range.

Return value

None (void).

Conditions and limits

The append returns no success value. If the whole record does not fit, it sets __vramq_overflow() to 1 and leaves existing records and length intact. Exact fits are accepted. An old overflow flag does not block an append that fits, so handle or reset the latch before using it to judge a new batch. A sequence of appends is not transactional.

__zapper_light

The default port-2 light reader. Calls the same helper as __zapper_light2().

Syntax

c
u8 __zapper_light(void);

Return value

1 when $4017 bit 3 is clear, otherwise 0. Port 1 is not read.

Conditions and limits

These APIs access $4016/$4017 directly. Do not interleave interrupt-driven gamepad, keyboard or serial operations on the same ports. Controller shift positions can also be affected. The sample disables NMI while capturing input, then enables it when initializing the display.

Reads the instantaneous signal. It does not strobe, wait for a frame, detect an edge, locate an aim point or decide a hit. Separate raw and trigger/light calls each read the register at their own time, so their values can differ while the signal changes.

The light input is active-low: a clear bit 3 produces a return value of one. That conversion does not detect whether a gun is connected; a gamepad or unconnected input may also yield one. Drawing a target on screen does not turn this into a hit-testing API.

Bit conversion is also unit-tested in an owned test ROM by redirecting register reads to RAM fixture values. The tests cover 00/08/10/18 combinations with unrelated bits set. This unit test is separate from the unmodified sample run and from real peripheral behavior.

These images run the downloadable ROMs unchanged in KUROSAKI. Its current input bus models gamepads but not keyboard, light-gun or serial-adapter signals. The external input bits read as zero, so the captures do not verify those devices. Physical key input, optical sensing and communication remain untested.

NESdev: Zapper

Usage example

c
#include "fc_ports_scene.h"
void main(void){
    __irq_disable();__ppu_ctrl_set(0);port_phase=1;
    port_result[0]=__zapper_raw1();port_result[1]=__zapper_trigger1();port_result[2]=__zapper_light1();
    port_result[3]=__zapper_raw2();port_result[4]=__zapper_trigger2();port_result[5]=__zapper_light2();
    port_result[6]=__zapper_trigger();port_result[7]=__zapper_light();
    port_phase=2;port_result[31]=165;
    m_init();m_text(2,2,"LIGHT-GUN INPUT SNAPSHOT");m_wait();
    m_text(2,5,"PORT   RAW  TRIGGER  LIGHT");m_wait();
    m_put(3,8,'1');port_hex(9,8,port_result[0]);port_number(15,8,port_result[1]);port_number(24,8,port_result[2]);m_wait();
    m_put(3,10,'2');port_hex(9,10,port_result[3]);port_number(15,10,port_result[4]);port_number(24,10,port_result[5]);m_wait();
    m_text(2,13,"DEFAULT = PORT 2");m_wait();
    m_text(2,15,"TRIGGER");port_number(15,15,port_result[6]);m_wait();
    m_text(2,17,"LIGHT");port_number(15,17,port_result[7]);m_wait();
    m_text(2,21,"LIGHT 1 IS NOT A HIT TEST");m_wait();
    while(1){m_wait();}
}

This is a calling fragment. Follow the stated initialization and buffer requirements before using it in a complete program.

Expected result

In KUROSAKI, both ports show RAW=00, TRIGGER=000 and LIGHT=001. The unsuffixed calls show the same 000/001 as port 2. LIGHT=001 comes from unmodeled input bit 3 reading zero, not from detecting screen brightness. The screen also states LIGHT 1 IS NOT A HIT TEST.

Complete example program

Build command

powershell
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force .\out | Out-Null
.\kitaqfc\kitaqfc.exe .\kitaq-docs\samples\api-examples\fc\peripheral_zapper.c -I .\kitaqfc\lib -I .\kitaq-docs\samples -o .\out\peripheral_zapper.nes --mapper=nrom --nes-chr=.\kitaq-docs\samples\font.chr --no-cache --no-disasm
.\kurosaki\kurosaki.exe run .\out\peripheral_zapper.nes --frames 120 --png .\out\peripheral_zapper.png

Declaration notes (original source)
Famicom/NES expansion input devices.
D1 readers are for expansion-port controllers/joysticks that expose a
standard 8-bit joypad stream on data line D1 instead of D0.
__joypad2p_voice() / __mic_read2p() return the Famicom 2P microphone bit.
/
Latch and read an eight-button stream from port-1 data line D1 rather than D0.
u8 __pad_read1_d1(void);
Latch and read an eight-button stream from port-2 data line D1 rather than D0.
u8 __pad_read2_d1(void);
Alias the port-1 D1 controller reader; the attached device must use the expected serial protocol.
u8 __exp_pad_read1(void);
Alias the port-2 D1 controller reader; this is not an expansion-device discovery operation.
u8 __exp_pad_read2(void);
Return controller-port 4016 bit 2 normalized to 0 or 1; this is a microphone level bit, not PCM audio.
u8 __joypad2p_voice(void);
Alias the same normalized microphone input bit as __joypad2p_voice.
u8 __mic_read2p(void);

 Zapper / light gun. The no-suffix names default to the usual port-2/Famicom
expansion-port mapping. __zapper_light*() returns 1 when light is detected.
/
Return raw 4016 & 18, retaining trigger and active-low light bits.

__zapper_trigger

The default port-2 trigger reader. Calls the same helper as __zapper_trigger2().

Syntax

c
u8 __zapper_trigger(void);

Return value

The normalized $4017 bit 4. It never automatically switches to port 1.

Conditions and limits

These APIs access $4016/$4017 directly. Do not interleave interrupt-driven gamepad, keyboard or serial operations on the same ports. Controller shift positions can also be affected. The sample disables NMI while capturing input, then enables it when initializing the display.

Reads the instantaneous signal. It does not strobe, wait for a frame, detect an edge, locate an aim point or decide a hit. Separate raw and trigger/light calls each read the register at their own time, so their values can differ while the signal changes.

The result is the trigger line’s logical state. It does not guarantee that the trigger remains fully pulled, and switch behavior depends on the device. For a game firing event, compare with the previous reading to detect the desired transition.

Bit conversion is also unit-tested in an owned test ROM by redirecting register reads to RAM fixture values. The tests cover 00/08/10/18 combinations with unrelated bits set. This unit test is separate from the unmodified sample run and from real peripheral behavior.

These images run the downloadable ROMs unchanged in KUROSAKI. Its current input bus models gamepads but not keyboard, light-gun or serial-adapter signals. The external input bits read as zero, so the captures do not verify those devices. Physical key input, optical sensing and communication remain untested.

csharp
EmitHelperStart("__zapper_trigger2");
            EmitNormalizeBoolFromMask(0x4017, 0x10, false);
        void EmitNormalizeBoolFromMask(int port, int mask, bool invert)
        {
            string zero = NewGeneratedLabel("bool_zero");
            string done = NewGeneratedLabel("bool_done");
            EmitAsm("LDA", Mem(port));
            EmitAsm("AND", Imm(mask));
            if (invert) EmitAsm("BNE", Rel(zero)); else EmitAsm("BEQ", Rel(zero));
            EmitAsm("LDA", Imm(1));
            EmitAsm("JMP", Abs(done));
            _assembly.Add(Expr.Make(Tag.Label, zero));
            EmitAsm("LDA", Imm(0));
            _assembly.Add(Expr.Make(Tag.Label, done));
            EmitAsm("RTS");
        }
